records.content:
This book documents the TAMBI project, a computational psychiatry study of how people infer hidden structure in an uncertain environment, and of how this inference relates to symptoms of anxiety, intolerance of uncertainty, depression and obsessive-compulsive symptoms. It contains the task, the analysis pipeline, the computational model and its validation, and the current results, and it is the reference for anyone who joins the project or needs to reproduce an analysis.

Note

Status of this page: 10 October 2026. Behavioural N = 68 (C1 = 24, C2 = 30, C3 = 14), questionnaire analyses N = 65 (C1 = 23, C2 = 29, C3 = 13), from the analysis run of 8 October 2026 (run tag 09_09). Data collection is ongoing, with a target of N = 90 to 100. The study is exploratory and not preregistered; targeted tests are to be preregistered for the planned online replication.

records.content:
RQ1. Does instruction about the latent structure change how participants infer it? The three instruction conditions differ in what participants are told about the task structure, and the question is whether this shifts behaviour from gradual, outcome-driven learning toward inference about the latent state.

RQ2. Are questionnaire scores associated with how participants infer the latent structure? The focal measures are state and trait anxiety, intolerance of uncertainty, depression and obsessive-compulsive symptoms, which are always analysed alongside each other.

RQ3. Does a latent-state model describe the behaviour, and do its parameters reflect the behavioural measures? This concerns the six-parameter inference agent, its validation, and the relation of its parameters to behaviour and questionnaires.

records.content:
Task

Mosquito Defense Task, a spatial predictive-inference task implemented in PsychoPy. On each trial, participants place 7 nets on 32 positions of a circle to intercept an attack after one of two colour cues.

Latent structure

Two latent states alternate across nine episodes of 16 to 24 trials. At each transition, the attack directions of both cues rotate by 120°. The direction for the second cue is 70° from that for the first.

Events

Oddballs (about 10% of trials, attack 120° from the current target without a change of state) and omissions (about 10% of trials, no attack shown).

Manipulation

Three instruction conditions, between participants. C1: how to place nets. C2: additionally, that rules might determine the attack direction. C3: additionally, the cue offset and the rotation.

Questionnaires

STICSA (state and trait), IU-18, BDI-II, OCI-12 (focal); ERS, PCL-5, SIAS, ACE, EAT-26 (wider battery).

Further data

Eye tracking (EyeLink 1000), pupil size, mouse tracking, physiology (BIOPAC), in-task affect ratings.

Computational model

A two-state hidden Markov model with von Mises emissions and six free parameters, fitted by amortized simulation-based inference (BayesFlow), preceded by an amortized comparison of five candidate models.

Each participant contributes three data streams that the analyses bring together: the trial-by-trial behaviour (net allocations) and the measures derived from it, the questionnaire scores, and the posterior distributions of the six model parameters. Eye-tracking, pupil, mouse-tracking and physiological data are analysed in separate sub-projects.

Participant flow (recruitment, exclusions, and the sample size at each stage) is not documented in this book. It is maintained during data collection in the shared project folder on Google Drive, which is the single source for these numbers.

records.content: Julia (doctoral researcher, on-site study lead), Ondřej Zika (primary supervisor, University College Dublin), Tina Lonsdorf (principal investigator, Lonsdorf Lab), Claudia Massaccesi (collaborator), Oscar (eye-tracking sub-project).
tba

This chapter documents the analysis layer that connects the three data streams the project produces about each participant: the behavioural data (and its GLMM-derived summaries), the BayesFlow-inferred computational parameters, and the questionnaire scores. The three connection-level chapters — 

Symptom → Behaviour, 

Symptom → Parameters, and 

Parameters ↔ Behaviour — cross-reference back to the shared design decisions documented here, in the same way the behavioural model chapters reference 

Cross Cutting Methods.

The shared foundation is implemented in integration_common.py; the three connection-level analyses are symptom_behavior_models.py, symptom_parameter_models.py, and parameter_behavior_models.py.

By the time a participant has been through the pipeline, three quite different descriptions of them exist. The behavioural pipeline (

Primary GLMMs, and the raw descriptive markers) yields summary statistics and a handful of GLMM-derived per-participant scalars (cue-dissociation rate, evidence-dependence slope, rule-applier class, discovery episode, the Rule-1 marker). The amortized inference pipeline (

The Inference Agent, 

Amortized Bayesian Inference) yields six parameter posteriors per participant. The questionnaire pipeline yields the trait and symptom scales.

Each of these was, until this layer was added, analysed largely in isolation. The integration layer closes that gap and merges the seperate data streams in a single place and under one coherent methodological umbrella. It exists to answer three families of question:

Do symptoms predict behaviour? - 

Symptom → Behaviour.

Do symptoms predict the computational parameters? - 

Symptom → Parameters.

Do the computational parameters track the behaviour they are meant to, and do they mediate any symptom→behaviour link? (construct validity and mechanism) - 

Parameters ↔ Behaviour.

Within the integration pipeline, all three connection-level scripts obtain their data from a single function, integration_common.build_master_table, which assembles one per-participant table from whatever streams are available. This was implemented to prevent that each script re-implements its own merge, with its own ID matching and its own column conventions.

Stream

Source

Contents

Instruction condition

behavioural results

the ordered condition factor + its condition_L / condition_Q contrasts

Model-independent features

feature_extraction.py

the 54 features (allocation shape, oddball/transition/omission reaction, cue differentiation, dynamics)

Behavioural summary

build_behavioral_summary

defense rate, angular error, entropy, placement speed, state-affect means/slopes

GLMM-derived scalars

statistical-analysis output dir

cue-dissociation rate, evidence-dependence slope, rule-applier class, discovery episode, Rule-1 marker

BayesFlow parameters

all_participants_posteriors.csv

the six parameter posterior means and per-parameter posterior SDs

Questionnaire scores

questionnaire_scores.csv

trait/symptom totals and subscales

Every stream is optional except the behavioural results, which anchor participant identity and the instruction condition. Streams that are absent are simply omitted; the table contains whatever could be assembled. The condition contrasts are reconstructed here using the same orthogonal-polynomial coding documented in 

Cross Cutting Methods, so that condition moderation tests in the integration layer are coded identically to the behavioural GLMMs.

The original design envisaged consuming the GLMM random-effect BLUPs (per-participant slopes for oddball reactivity, transition reactivity, generalisation, and so on) as the individual-difference measures linking behaviour to the other layers — this is the approach documented in 

Factor Structure.

At the current N, however, every model in the behavioural pipeline falls back to ols_cluster_robust or mixedlm_full without an estimable random-effect covariance, so no M*_blups.csv files are produced. The integration layer therefore builds on the GLMM-derived scalar outputs instead (cue-dissociation rate, evidence-dependence slope, rule-applier class, discovery episode, the Rule-1 marker) which are computed directly and do not depend on a random-effect structure being estimable. The harvest routine will pick up M*_blups.csv automatically if they ever appear (e.g. at the target N, when models (hopefully) converge with random slopes), with no code change required.

records.content:
The current N is small (≈34) and the target is N ≈ 90–100. Corrections are therefore deliberately light-touch, on the reasoning that effects which are marginal at the current N are expected to firm up toward the target rather than to be artefacts, and over-correcting now would discard them prematurely and thus complicating the preliminary interpretation within the data collection phase. Concretely:

Primary families: small sets of theory-motivated, directional tests (e.g. H1 anxiety → noise_reactivity; the parameter↔behaviour convergent-validity pairings). These are corrected, if at all, within their own small family using Holm (family-wise control is the appropriate frame for a handful of directional primary tests), and are reported uncorrected alongside.

Exploratory grids: the full trait × metric and parameter × feature matrices. These get Benjamini–Hochberg FDR and are labelled explicitly as hypothesis-generating.

Every correction in the code carries an inline comment stating which family it belongs to and why. The aim is that a reader (and myself whenever I come back to the code in the future) can always tell whether a reported effect came from a small directional family or from a large exploratory grid.

The internalizing scales are strongly inter-correlated (trait anxiety, intolerance of uncertainty, depression, emotion-regulation difficulty all load on a shared internalizing dimension; the pairwise correlations in this sample run roughly 0.5–0.8). This is expected and is consistent with the broader literature, but it has a direct methodological consequence for this layer, since bivariate trait → parameter and trait → behaviour correlations are not, on their own, interpretable as evidence for a specific trait, because the shared internalizing variance is attributed to whichever scale is entered.

The integration scripts therefore report partial correlations (each trait controlling for the others) alongside the bivariate results, and the partial results should be treated as the more informative readout when asking whether a specific construct drives an association vs. a more general, potentially transdiagnostic factor. See 

Symptom → Parameters for a worked example where a bivariate-null association (trait anxiety → noise_reactivity) becomes the strongest signal in the table once the shared internalizing variance is partialled out.

This chapter documents the analysis that links the BayesFlow-inferred parameters to the behavioural data, on two levels, with statistical models rather than correlations and visualisation alone (the latter being what behavioral_validation.py already provides). It is implemented in parameter_behavior_models.py and draws its data from the canonical master table described in 

Cross-layer Integration: Overview.

The chapter answers two questions. First, construct validity: does each inferred parameter track the behavioural signature it is meant to, in the direction the generative model implies? Second, mechanism: does a parameter mediate any symptom → behaviour relationship?

Every prediction in this chapter is anchored to the parameter semantics defined in 

The Inference Agent. Two of the six parameters have a direction that is easy to invert, and inverting it turns a confirmation into an apparent contradiction:

Two parameters whose behavioural direction is counter-intuitive

noise_reactivity: high values mean surprises (i.e. oddballs) are attributed to noise, which produces weaker learning from oddballs and therefore a smaller oddball-driven behavioural shift. (Low values attribute surprises to state change → strong learning → larger shift.) So higher noise_reactivity predicts a smaller oddball shift.

belief_momentum: high values mean inertia in latent-state inference: sluggish adaptation, slow state switching. So higher belief_momentum predicts a smaller and slower post-transition belief revision, not a faster one.

Level A regresses each behavioural feature on each parameter (participant-level OLS, standardised, controlling for condition), across the full feature set: the 54 features from feature_extraction.py plus the summary and GLMM-derived metrics used in the behavioural pipeline. The grid is corrected with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR as an exploratory family.

The dominant Level A pattern in the current data is that precision_weighting and belief_momentum load on overlapping allocation-shape and tracking features, with opposite signs:

precision_weighting → low entropy, high stacking, few slots occupied (β up to ±0.84).

belief_momentum → high tracking error, high circular variance, low cue-dissociation, smaller post-transition shift.

This opposite-sign pattern is expected, not an identifiability problem

A participant with high precision_weighting (concentrates the allocation tightly) and low belief_momentum (switches state readily when reversal evidence accumulates) is a tight, agile, structure-using learner; the opposite participant is diffuse and sluggish. These are opposite ends of two distinct parameters that nonetheless co-vary across participants because cognitive / learning phenotypes load on both. The parameters control genuinely different behavioural signatures, confirmed by the parameter-recovery sweeps documented in 

The Inference Agent and model_behavior_extended.py, which show clean, separable recovery and distinct behavioural effects when each parameter is varied with the others held fixed. The correlation seen here is therefore a property of the participants (a real phenotype covariance), not of the inference (parameter confusion).

Each pairing is tested by Spearman correlation with a one-sided p in the predicted direction and a within-family Holm flag. Holm is applied only within this small primary family, not folded into the Level A exploratory grid.

The last three pairings are the convergent-validity checks for the two parameters added after the original four. They are different in spirit from the symptom-driven hypotheses. Rather than testing a clinical prediction, they ask whether each new parameter does, behaviourally, what the model says it does. cue_sensitivity should manifest as a larger learned cue offset and cleaner cue dissociation, since that is precisely the associative quantity it scales, and placement_noise should manifest as greater undirected within-state scatter, since that is the action-level variability it was introduced to absorb. These are the most direct behavioural footprints any of the parameters have, so they serve as a sanity check on the inference as much as a substantive finding.

h_switch is the parameter with the weakest behavioural grounding here, since it acts on the timescale of the latent-state belief trajectory (z_prob drift), which does not map cleanly onto any single static summary feature the way the other three parameters do. Its convergent-validity pairings are correspondingly the most tentative.

The final module asks whether a parameter mediates a symptom → behaviour relationship. For a small set of theory-motivated triples (ADD LIST), it estimates the standard product-of-coefficients indirect effect with a bias-corrected bootstrap confidence interval, on standardised variables. This complements the trait → state → behaviour mediation already in behavior_questionnaire_integration.py by putting the computational parameter in the mediator role.

This chapter documents the models that use questionnaire (trait / symptom) scores as predictors of behavioural metrics, which is the most direct analysis level for the internalizing and anxiety hypotheses. It is implemented in symptom_behavior_models.py and draws its data from the master table described in 

Cross-layer Integration: Overview.

What this integration layer contributes is proper regression with covariate control, condition moderation, both a participant-level (two-stage) and a trial-level (hierarchical) route, and outcome-appropriate models for the categorical and temporal behavioural targets.

The behavioural outcomes fall into three families:

Model-independent summary metrics, namely defense rate, mean angular error, net entropy, placement speed; one continuous value per participant.

GLMM-derived per-participant scalars, namely cue-dissociation rate, evidence-dependence slope, the Rule-1 marker (post-transition belief shift). These are the individual-difference measures distilled by the behavioural pipeline (see 

Primary GLMMs).

Categorical / temporal outcomes, which include the rule-applier class (modelled by logistic regression) and discovery episode (related to traits by rank correlation, given the small applier subsample)

For every (trait, target) pair, two participant-level OLS models are fit on standardised variables:target ~ trait                          [+ covariates]      (main effect)
target ~ trait * condition_L            [+ covariates]      (moderation)

The first asks whether the trait predicts the behavioural metric; the second asks whether that relationship is moderated by instruction depth (a trait : condition_L interaction). Covariates (age, sex) are included when present in the merged table. The full trait x target grid of main-effect tests is corrected with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR as an exploratory family; the interaction tests are corrected as a separate family because they answer a different question. Both the main-effect and interaction FDR families are flagged hypothesis-generating.

Why both a two-stage and a hierarchical route

The two-stage approach collapses each participant to one summary value and is transparent and robust. The hierarchical approach uses all trials and a participant random intercept, which is more powerful but heavier and, importantly, requires care in interpretation when the predictor of interest varies only between participants. The two are offered together so they can be read against each other.

For a small set of headline trial-level outcomes (angular_error_deg, defense_rate), the script additionally fits a mixed model with the trait as a between-participant (level-2) predictor:trial_outcome ~ trait_z + condition_L + (1 | participant)

using mixedlm for the Gaussian outcome and BinomialBayesMixedGLM (variational Bayes) for the per-trial binary outcome. These fit where feasible and record their fit method and convergence; some are tight at the current N and fall back gracefully.

Interpreting the hierarchical fixed effects

When a between-participant predictor (a trait, constant within participant) is entered into a trial-level mixed model with thousands of trials, the standard error on that predictor can be driven down by trial-level variance that is unrelated to the between-participant contrast, producing implausibly small p-values. In the current run with N = 34, the hierarchical defense_rate models returned highly “significant” trait effects (e.g. IU → defense rate, p < 10⁻⁵) that are entirely absent from the two-stage analysis on the same data. Where the two routes disagree this sharply, the two-stage estimate is the honest readout of the between-participant relationship, and the hierarchical fixed effect should be treated with suspicion until the random-effect structure has been checked (e.g. confirming the trait coefficient is stable when the model is reduced to a random intercept only). The hierarchical models are retained for the headline outcomes but are not, at present, the basis for any between-participant trait claim.

Rule-applier class is reduced to a binary indicator (immediate or late applier = 1) and modelled by logistic regression on each trait, controlling for condition:rule_applier_is_applier ~ trait_z + condition_L

This asks whether a trait raises or lowers the odds of applying the structural rule, over and above the instruction manipulation. The exploratory family is FDR-corrected.

Discovery episode (when an applier first reliably applies the rule) is related to traits by Spearman correlation, restricted to the applier subsample. This is the analysis that speaks to the hypothesis that a stronger tendency to find patterns may come with earlier discovery (and may relate to mental-health measures). It is deliberately not FDR-corrected, since at the pilot N the applier subsample is tiny (often well under ten) but might still be insightful to already investigate to eventually control for interactions in future analyses, so this is purely descriptive / hypothesis-generating and is flagged as such, to be revisited at the target N.

At N = 32 the two-stage main effects are uniformly modest and none survive FDR, which is obviously not suprising. However, the value of running this layer now is in establishing the pipeline and the operationalisations, not in the any point estimates.

This chapter documents the models that use questionnaire (trait / symptom) scores as predictors of the BayesFlow-inferred computational parameters. It is implemented in symptom_parameter_models.py and draws its data from the canonical master table described in 

Cross-layer Integration: Overview.

What this integration layer contributes is regression with covariate control, condition moderation, partial correlations, and parameter-uncertainty weighting, organised around a small set of theory-motivated primary hypotheses (to be discussed!).

records.content:
The parameters and their semantics are defined fully in 

The Inference Agent; they are summarised here only insofar as the directional hypotheses depend on getting their meaning exactly right.

The agent has six parameters in total, but the symptom-driven hypotheses concern only the four original ones, listed below. The two parameters added later, cue_sensitivity and placement_noise, were mainly introduced for reasons internal to the model (isolating associative cue learning and absorbing undirected within-state placement scatter, respectively) and neither carries an a-priori clinical prediction (to be discussed - however, the prediction would not be a priori atp). cue_sensitivity is in fact expected to eventually dissociate from the internalizing scales (it indexes a learning ability rather than an affective bias), and placement_noise is an execution-noise term. Both are still entered into the exploratory trait x parameter grid further down, but they do not appear among the primary hypotheses, and the current empirical results (N = 34) bear this out: neither shows a meaningful correlation with any questionnaire scale.

Parameter

Meaning

Direction that matters

precision_weighting

allocation concentration / stacking

high → tighter, more concentrated placement

noise_reactivity

stochasticity-attribution bias (Piray & Daw)

high → surprises attributed to noise → weaker learning

belief_momentum

inertia in latent-state inference

high → sluggish state switching

h_switch

perceived environmental volatility

high → readier to entertain a state change

The two emphasised rows are the ones whose direction is counter-intuitive from the name alone, and getting them backwards inverts every downstream prediction - a clarification worth stating explicitly here because it is easy to get confused here (this is of course not stated because it is driven by my own experience - would never happen to me for sure).

records.content:
The three primary hypotheses

H1 (Piray & Daw, 2021): trait anxiety (STICSA-T) → lower noise_reactivity. Anxious participants over-attribute surprising outcomes to genuine structural change rather than to noise, i.e. they have a lower noise-attribution setting.

H2 (Zika et al., 2023): intolerance of uncertainty (IU-18) → higher belief_momentum. Difficulty tolerating uncertainty manifests as reluctance to commit to a stable state belief, i.e. sluggish, inertial state inference.

H3 (volatility over-estimation): intolerance of uncertainty → higher h_switch. Over-estimation of how often the environment changes.

Each is a single directional prediction, tested with a Spearman correlation, a two-sided p, a one-sided p in the predicted direction, and a within-family Holm flag. Holm (family-wise) is applied only within this three-member family, since these are the primary tests and are not folded into the exploratory grid, which would over-penalise them at current N (to be discussed how to adjust this at final N).

For every (trait, parameter) pair the script fits, on standardised variables:parameter ~ trait                       [+ covariates]      (main effect)
parameter ~ trait * condition_L         [+ covariates]      (moderation)

and, where a posterior SD column ({param}_std) is available, a precision-weighted main-effect model with weights 1/\text{SD}^2, so that participants whose parameter is poorly identified contribute less. The weighted estimate is reported alongside the unweighted one. The full main-effect grid is FDR-corrected as an exploratory family.

Because the internalizing scales are strongly inter-correlated (see 

overview), the script computes partial Spearman correlations between each anxiety-core trait and each parameter, controlling for the other core traits. This separates the unique contribution of, say, intolerance of uncertainty from general trait anxiety. The partial results are the more informative readout when the question is whether or which specific construct drives an association or if the effect is potentially driven by a transdiagnostic latent factor; the exploratory family is FDR-corrected.

At N = 32 the three primary hypotheses behave as follows. H2 (IU → belief_momentum) and H3 (IU → h_switch) reach one-sided significance uncorrected (p₁ ≈ 0.04 and ≈ 0.06) but do not survive within-family Holm; H1 (STICSA-T → noise_reactivity) is null at the bivariate level (r ≈ −0.19).

The instructive result is what the partial correlations reveal. Once the shared internalizing variance is removed, STICSA-T → noise_reactivity becomes the strongest single association in the table (partial r ≈ −0.37, p ≈ 0.04), i.e. the H1 effect is present but is masked at the bivariate level by IU-loaded shared variance. Within the exploratory regression grid, the inhibitory subscale of IU carries the strongest association with belief_momentum (β ≈ 0.43), more than the prospective subscale, which is theoretically coherent, since inhibitory IU (the action-paralysing facet) maps naturally onto reluctance to commit to a new state.

None of these survive multiplicity correction at the current N, and none should be reported as established. They are recorded here as the associations most likely to firm up toward the target N, and as a demonstration that the partial-correlation step changes which trait looks responsible for a given parameter association. So please take all of this with a grain of salt :)

This chapter summarises the latent-state model: its generative assumptions, its six free parameters, and the way the parameters are estimated and validated. It gives the defining equations only. Derivations, all constants and the complete update rules are in 

The Inference Agent and in 

Notation, Priors and Fixed Constants.

Status

The equations describe the agent that produced the current results (run 09_09), that is, reduced_agent_v3.py before the two-stage allocation patch of 10 October 2026. The posterior network of that run was trained on 50,000 simulations with the 40 summary features of feature_extraction.py. A network with the two-stage allocation, 100,000 simulations and the 54 features of feature_extraction_v3.py is being trained; the recovery and calibration values below do not apply to it.

The model is a two-state hidden Markov model with von Mises emissions on the circle of 32 slots. An agent filters the latent state trial by trial, tracks the attack directions with gated delta-rule updates, and converts its predictive distribution into an allocation of seven nets. Six parameters govern this process. Because the mapping from parameters to allocations has no closed-form likelihood, the parameters are estimated by amortized simulation-based inference: a neural network is trained once on simulated sessions and then returns the posterior distribution for each participant.

Latent state. A binary state z_t \in \{0, 1\} determines which of two attack regimes is active. Before each outcome, the belief is propagated with the switch probability h:p_t^{\text{pred}}(z = 1) = p_{t-1}(z = 1)\,(1 - h) + \big[1 - p_{t-1}(z = 1)\big]\,h .

Emissions. Given the state, the attack direction \omega_t follows a two-component von Mises mixture. The regular component is centred on the believed direction \hat{\mu}_{c,z} for cue c in state z, and the oddball component is displaced by the believed rotation \hat{\Delta}:L^{(z)} = (1 - \rho_{\text{eff}})\, f_{\text{vM}}(\omega_t;\, \hat{\mu}_{c,z}, \kappa_{\text{fixed}})
          + \rho_{\text{eff}}\, f_{\text{vM}}(\omega_t;\, \hat{\mu}_{c,z} + \hat{\Delta}, \kappa_{\text{fixed}}),
\qquad \rho_{\text{eff}} = \rho_{\text{fixed}} \cdot \text{nr} .

State update. The state belief is updated by exact forward filtering and then smoothed with the belief momentum \text{bm}:p_t^{\text{Bayes}}(z = 1) =
\frac{p_t^{\text{pred}}(z = 1)\, L^{(1)}}
     {p_t^{\text{pred}}(z = 0)\, L^{(0)} + p_t^{\text{pred}}(z = 1)\, L^{(1)}},
\qquad
p_t(z = 1) = (1 - \text{bm})\, p_t^{\text{Bayes}}(z = 1) + \text{bm}\, p_{t-1}(z = 1) .

Direction updates. The directions are point estimates. The direction of the dominant state \hat{z}_t is updated by a delta rule whose step is reduced when the outcome is attributed to the oddball component:\hat{\mu} \leftarrow \hat{\mu} + \eta_\mu \, g_t \, \text{PE}_t,
\qquad
\eta_\mu = c_\eta \cdot \text{pw},
\qquad
g_t = 1 - \frac{\rho_{\text{eff}}\, L_{\text{odd}}^{(\hat{z}_t)}}
               {(1 - \rho_{\text{eff}})\, L_{\text{reg}}^{(\hat{z}_t)} + \rho_{\text{eff}}\, L_{\text{odd}}^{(\hat{z}_t)}} ,

with \text{PE}_t = \angle(\omega_t - \hat{\mu}_{c_t, \hat{z}_t}) and c_\eta = 0.10. On a trial on which the dominant state changes, the direction is realigned to the outcome with rate \max(\eta_\mu, 0.85) and without gating. The offset between the two cues, \hat{\delta}_B, is learned from cue B outcomes and is drawn toward the target \text{cs} \cdot 70°, so that its steady-state value scales with the cue sensitivity \text{cs}.

Predictive distribution and action. The predictive distribution over the slots mixes the two states with weights that commit to the more probable state,\pi_s \propto \sum_{z \in \{0,1\}} w_z
\Big[(1 - \rho_{\text{eff}})\, f_{\text{vM}}(\phi_s;\, \hat{\mu}_{c,z}, \kappa_{\text{eff}})
   + \rho_{\text{eff}}\, f_{\text{vM}}(\phi_s;\, \hat{\mu}_{c,z} + \hat{\Delta}, \kappa_{\text{eff}})\Big],
\qquad
w_1 = \sigma\!\big(8\,[\,p_t^{\text{pred}}(z = 1) - 0.5\,]\big),\quad w_0 = 1 - w_1 ,

where \kappa_{\text{eff}} = \kappa_{\text{fixed}} \cdot \text{pw} and \sigma is the logistic function. The distribution is shifted on the circle by a draw from \mathcal{N}(0, \text{pn}^2), raised to the power 1 + \text{pw}, renormalised, and converted into seven nets by largest-remainder rounding.

Two constants are fixed for all participants: \kappa_{\text{fixed}} = 4.0 and \rho_{\text{fixed}} = 0.10. The likelihoods of the belief update use \kappa_{\text{fixed}}; only the predictive distribution is scaled by \text{pw}.

All priors are independent and uniform. The recovery correlation r is the correlation between true values and posterior means in 300 simulations (network of 8 June 2026).

Precision weighting enters at three points by design, so that a higher value yields a narrower predictive distribution, a more concentrated allocation and faster direction learning. The three effects cannot be separated within this model.

Step

Procedure

Simulate

Parameters are drawn from the priors, one of the 20 trial schedules is drawn at random, and the agent is run on it.

Summarise

Each simulated session is reduced to a fixed vector of summary features. The same code computes the features of simulated and of participants’ sessions.

Train

A conditional density estimator q_\phi(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}) (flow matching with a small summary network, BayesFlow 2) is trained on the pairs of parameters and features (

Radev et al., 2020; 

Radev et al., 2023).

Apply

For each participant, 4,000 posterior samples are drawn conditional on the participant’s features. No further fitting takes place.

Before the parameters are interpreted, an amortized classifier compares the model with four alternatives (random allocation, two tracking models without latent states, and coverage of both state directions without state inference). The parameters are meant to be interpreted only for participants for whom the latent-state model has the highest posterior probability (

Model Comparison).

The summary features are not sufficient statistics. Whether they carry enough information about each parameter is an empirical question, which the recovery and calibration analyses answer.

Calibration. In simulation-based calibration (

Talts et al., 2018) with 500 simulations, the ranks of precision weighting, belief momentum and the switch probability show no deviation from uniformity in mean or dispersion. Cue sensitivity (rank mean 544, expected 499.5) and placement noise (rank mean 467) deviate, and the rank dispersion of noise reactivity is elevated. These deviations have not yet been examined with a graphical test.

Recovery. Recovery is high for precision weighting, placement noise, cue sensitivity and belief momentum, moderate for the switch probability, and low for noise reactivity (table above).

Posterior predictive checks compare participants’ features with features simulated from their posteriors (

Posterior Predictive Checks).

The details are in 

Amortized Bayesian Inference. The analyses that are still missing are listed on the 

front page.

Noise reactivity is weakly identified. In the agent described here, the oddball component of the predictive distribution receives almost no nets after sharpening, so that \rho_{\text{eff}} has little effect on the allocations. No conclusion is drawn from associations with this parameter. The two-stage allocation addresses this and is being evaluated.

The switch probability is bounded by saturation. Above h = \rho_{\text{eff}} a single oddball changes the dominant state, and higher values produce nearly the same behaviour. The upper bound of the prior reflects this (

h_switch Identifiability).

The model comparison is confounded with action noise. Among the directed models, only the latent-state model has placement noise and cue sensitivity. A comparison with matched action noise is outstanding.

Estimates near the prior bounds. Posterior samples are clipped to the prior bounds, and several participants have estimates of the switch probability, cue sensitivity and placement noise close to a bound.

Feature set and network behind the current results

The results of run 09_09 were obtained with networks trained on 8 June 2026 with the 40 summary features of feature_extraction.py (posterior network: 50,000 simulations; model classifier: 40,000 simulations). Where this chapter refers to 54 features (feature_extraction_v3.py) or to 

105 simulations, it describes the network that has been in training since 10 October 2026. Details: 

Fitting the Models to Participant Data.

Formally, we seek the posterior:p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}) \propto p(\mathbf{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}) \cdot p(\boldsymbol{\theta})

where \boldsymbol{\theta} = (\text{pw}, \text{nr}, \text{bm}, h, \text{cs}, \text{pn}) \in \mathbb{R}^6 are the cognitive parameters (precision_weighting, noise_reactivity, belief_momentum, h_switch, cue_sensitivity, placement_noise) and \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{54} is the feature vector. Rather than computing this posterior analytically or via sampling, we train a conditional density estimator q_\phi(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}) parameterized by neural network weights \phi to approximate p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}) across the full joint space (\boldsymbol{\theta}, \mathbf{x}). The priors p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) and all fixed constants of the simulator are listed in one place in Notation, Priors and Fixed Constants.

We approximated the posterior using neural posterior estimation (NPE) with learned summary statistics (

Radev et al., 2020), as implemented in the BayesFlow 2.0 framework for amortized Bayesian inference (

Radev et al., 2023a).

Specificially, the implemented inference pipeline uses the following architecture:



Figure 1:The Amortized Bayesian Inference Workflow.Agent Simulation → Feature Extraction → DeepSet(64) → FlowMatching → Posterior
     (CPU)            (deterministic)     (summary)    (inference)   (6 params)

Summary Network: A DeepSet (

Zaheer et al., 2017) maps the 54-dimensional feature vector (reshaped to a 1-element set) to a 64-dimensional summary representation. The DeepSet architecture is used (instead of an MLP) to comply with BayesFlow’s internal architecture requirements for condition passing. With a single set element it is functionally an MLP encoder of the feature vector and should be read as such.\mathbf{h} = \text{DeepSet}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^{64}

Inference Network: FlowMatching (

Lipman et al., 2022; 

2024) with optimal transport and an MLP subnet (4 layers × 256 units, 5% dropout) learns a conditional normalizing flow from the 64-dimensional summary to the 6-dimensional posterior over parameters. FlowMatching was chosen over coupling flows for its faster convergence and better handling of multimodal posteriors.

How this works: the 64-dimensional summary \mathbf{h} conditions a Flow Matching model that learns a continuous normalizing flow from a standard normal base distribution to the conditional posterior:\boldsymbol{\theta} = F_\phi(\mathbf{z}; \mathbf{h}), \quad \mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_6)

The flow F_\phi is parameterized by an MLP with 4 hidden layers of 256 units each, 5% dropout, and mish activation. We use optimal transport coupling (

Tong et al., 2023) to improve training efficiency.

The total number of trainable parameters is approximately 850,000.

The network is trained on 100,000 simulated sessions:

Data generation. N_{\text{train}} = 100{,}000 simulations are generated in parallel. For each simulation:

Parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} are drawn from the uniform priors

A trial schedule is randomly selected from the 20 available schedules

The agent runs the full session, producing allocations \{\mathbf{g}_t\}

The 54-dimensional feature vector \mathbf{x} is extracted

The pre-generated feature vectors are then used to train the DeepSet + FlowMatching network:

Training. The network is trained offline (i.e., on the pre-generated dataset, not with on-the-fly simulation) for up to 300 epochs with:

Batch size: 256

Initial learning rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}

Optimizer: Adam (this is the default Keras settings)

Early stopping: patience 50, restoring best weights (monitored on validation loss)

Validation split: 10% (10,000 held-out simulations)

Loss function. BayesFlow’s default training objective for Flow Matching is the conditional flow matching loss (

Lipman et al., 2022; 

2024), which minimizes the expected squared error between the learned and target velocity fields:\mathcal{L}(\phi) = \mathbb{E}_{t, \boldsymbol{\theta}, \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x}} \left[ \| v_\phi(t, \boldsymbol{\theta}_t; \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x})) - u_t(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t \mid \boldsymbol{\theta}) \|^2 \right]

where t \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1), \boldsymbol{\theta}_t = (1-t)\mathbf{z} + t\boldsymbol{\theta} (with optimal transport pairing), and u_t is the target velocity field.

How our loss curve looks like:



Figure 2:Training Loss and Validation Loss

To ensure both stability and validity of the inference pipeline, we run Simulation-Based Calibration (SBC) and Parameter Recoverability as complementary validation procedures. Both are produced by run_agent_v3.py --mode validate, which writes sbc.json, sbc.png, recovery.json and recovery.png. The numbers below are those of the current six-parameter network and replace all earlier values. The checks that are still missing (parameter cross-recovery, posterior correlations, graphical SBC, recovery in the empirical parameter range) are listed on the front page.

Following 

Talts et al. (2018), we verify posterior calibration via SBC. For M = 500 simulations with known parameters the posterior is sampled and the rank of the true parameter within the posterior is computed. Specificially, this is how the procedure works:

Draw \boldsymbol{\theta}^* \sim p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) from the prior

Simulate data \mathbf{x}^* from the agent with \boldsymbol{\theta}^*

Draw K = 1000 posterior samples \{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^K \sim q_\phi(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathbf{x}^*)

Compute the rank statistic: r_i = \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb{I}[\theta_i^{(k)} < \theta_i^*] for each parameter i

Under correct posterior calibration, r_i \sim \text{Discrete Uniform}(0, K), with mean K/2 = 500 and standard deviation \sqrt{((K+1)^2 - 1)/12} \approx 289. A rank mean that differs from 500 indicates a systematic shift of the posterior relative to the true value, and a rank standard deviation that differs from 289 indicates posteriors that are too narrow (larger than 289) or too wide (smaller than 289). With M = 500 simulations, the standard error of a rank mean is 289/\sqrt{500} \approx 12.9 and that of a rank standard deviation is approximately 5.8, and the last two columns of the table express each deviation in these units.

For precision_weighting, noise_reactivity, belief_momentum and h_switch, the rank means lie within half a standard error of the expected value, so that the posteriors of these four parameters show no systematic shift relative to the true values.

Two parameters deviate in their rank mean. For cue_sensitivity the rank mean of 544 lies 3.4 standard errors above the expected value, which means that the true value falls in the upper part of the posterior more often than calibration allows, that is, the posterior of cue_sensitivity is shifted downward relative to the true value. This is the direction expected from the boundary effect described in The Inference Agent, because posteriors of values near the upper bound of 1.0 cannot extend above the bound. For placement_noise the rank mean of 467 lies 2.5 standard errors below the expected value, so that its posterior is shifted upward relative to the true value. A corresponding boundary effect at the lower bound of 0 is a candidate explanation, but it has not been checked, and the earlier description of placement_noise as free of boundary effects does not hold for the current network.

The rank standard deviation exceeds its expected value for five of the six parameters, by 1.1 to 1.7 standard errors for four of them and by 3.0 standard errors for noise_reactivity. A rank standard deviation above the expected value arises when true values fall in the tails of the posterior too often, that is, when posteriors are somewhat too narrow. For noise_reactivity the posterior is therefore unbiased on average, but its width is, on this evidence, slightly underestimated, and the statement that its limited point recovery is fully reflected in appropriately wide credible intervals has to be qualified accordingly.

Rank means and standard deviations summarise only the first two moments of the rank distribution and do not locate a deviation within the parameter range. The rank histograms in the figure, and preferably empirical cumulative distribution function difference plots with simultaneous confidence bands (

Säilynoja et al., 2022), are needed to decide whether the deviations of cue_sensitivity and placement_noise are confined to the bounds and whether the excess rank dispersion of noise_reactivity is reliable. Both are open items.

We run 300 simulations with known parameters drawn from the prior. The posterior mean is compared to the true value. High correlation and low RMSE indicate reliable estimation. Because the correlation is computed over the full prior range, it describes recovery across that range and not specifically in the region occupied by participants.

The confidence intervals are Fisher-transformed intervals for n = 300, and the relative RMSE is the RMSE divided by the prior range. A second reference is the RMSE that would result from ignoring the data and reporting the prior mean, which equals the prior standard deviation (prior range divided by \sqrt{12}). Relative to that reference the RMSE is 0.09 (precision_weighting), 0.18 (placement_noise), 0.36 (cue_sensitivity), 0.40 (belief_momentum), 0.54 (h_switch) and 0.76 (noise_reactivity) of the prior standard deviation, so that the data reduce the estimation error of noise_reactivity by about a quarter and that of h_switch by about a half.

Five of the six parameters achieve recovery correlations of 0.82 or higher. Parameter recovery of this kind is the standard check that a model’s parameters can be estimated from data of the available size (

Wilson & Collins, 2019). The exception, noise_reactivity (r = 0.636), is weakly recovered. Its target behaviour (oddball attribution) is governed by few informative events per session, a third of which are diffuse or hedged responses rather than a clean stay-versus-follow decision (see Oddball-Response Diagnostics). In a matched random-forest screen, the addition of the action-level placement_noise parameter reduced the recovery of noise_reactivity by approximately 0.17 (from ≈ 0.63 with placement_noise fixed to ≈ 0.46 with it free) by veiling the action-level features that carry its signal, a dilution of signal rather than a confound between the two parameters, since their within-posterior correlation was ≈ 0. Accordingly, noise_reactivity is reported with its posterior uncertainty rather than as a point estimate, and no conclusion is currently drawn from associations that involve it. h_switch (r = 0.825) is the second weakest parameter, for the reason documented in h_switch Identifiability: above the switch threshold h > \rho_{\text{fixed}} \cdot \text{nr} the behaviour saturates.

The correlation of each true parameter with the estimates of the other five parameters (the parameter cross-recovery, or confusion, matrix) cannot be computed from recovery.json, which stores only the six diagonal correlations and the RMSEs. It requires the arrays of true values and posterior means, which run_agent_v3.py computes but does not save. This analysis is an open item.

For real participants, the pipeline:

Parses net allocations from the all_slot_barriers column of the behavioral results CSV

Extracts the trial schedule from the same file (episode, cue_identity, actual_vector_angle, outcome_occurred, is_oddball)

Computes the identical 54 features used during training

Passes the feature vector through the trained network

Returns 4,000 posterior samples per parameter, from which means, standard deviations, and credible intervals are computed*

Clips samples to prior bounds to prevent out-of-support estimates

*Posterior means, standard deviations, and central 95% credible intervals (the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles) are computed from the clipped samples. The SBC and recovery checks above use unclipped samples.

The results of run 09_09 were obtained with networks trained on 8 June 2026 with the 40 summary features of feature_extraction.py (posterior network: 50,000 simulations; model classifier: 40,000 simulations). Where this chapter refers to 54 features (feature_extraction_v3.py) or to

hierarchy.lvl2: Why we decided to take a feature-based approach
Why we decided to take a feature-based approach

records.content:
Rather than feeding the raw 32-slot allocation time series to the neural network (which caused training instability due to sparsity, variable sequence lengths, and the curse of dimensionality), we extract a fixed-size vector of 54 behavioral summary statistics per session. This approach eliminates variable-length padding issues, replaces sparse integer inputs with continuous, bounded features, ensures identical feature computation for simulated and real participant data (no domain shift) and thus reduces the neural network’s task from “learn to extract behavioral patterns from raw sequences” to “learn to map extracted patterns to parameters” - which also best aligns with the core research focus.

Furthermore, this approach simplifies the integration of multimodal data while maintaining the same network architecture; and - even more interestingly - it potentially allows for generalization to various tasks rather than being limited to a single paradigm.

All 54 features satisfy the following requirements (to ensure traceability and computational stability):

Continuous and bounded: No discrete or unbounded values that could destabilize training

Deterministic: Given the same allocation sequence \{\mathbf{g}_t\} and schedule, the features are identical

Domain-invariant: The same extraction code operates on both simulated agent output and real participant data (to avoid preprocessing differences that could create domain shift)

Information-preserving: Each feature is designed to capture a specific aspect of behavior that distinguishes between parameter values, based on prior sensitivity analysis (see The inference agent, associated behavioral features in the parameter definition section)

records.content:
The single direct marker for the belief-to-action execution noise parameter placement_noise. It measures undirected, memoryless placement scatter on stable mid-episode trials, separated from structured inference.

Feature

Description

within_state_placement_var

Mean absolute deviation of allocation from the local same-cue, same-episode circular mean on regular mid-episode trials (trial-in-episode > 4), in degrees

1. mean_net_entropy — Mean Shannon entropy (base 2) of the net allocation over all trials: \bar{H} = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T H(\mathbf{g}_t), where H(\mathbf{g}) = -\sum_s p_s \log_2 p_s and p_s = g_s / \sum_j g_j.

2. std_net_entropy — Standard deviation of per-trial entropy: \text{SD}(H(\mathbf{g}_1), \ldots, H(\mathbf{g}_T)).

3. mean_slots_occupied — Mean number of slots with \geq 1 net: \frac{1}{T} \sum_t |\{s : g_{t,s} > 0\}|.

4. mean_max_nets_slot — Mean maximum stacking depth: \frac{1}{T} \sum_t \max_s g_{t,s}.

5. frac_stacking — Fraction of trials where any slot has \geq 2 nets: \frac{1}{T} \sum_t \mathbb{I}[\max_s g_{t,s} \geq 2].

6. mean_circ_variance — Mean circular variance of the allocation: \bar{V} = \frac{1}{T} \sum_t (1 - R_t), where R_t = \|\sum_s p_s e^{i\phi_s}\| is the resultant length.

7. entropy_change_halves — Difference in mean entropy between the second and first halves of the session: \bar{H}_{t > T/2} - \bar{H}_{t \leq T/2}.

8. mean_angular_error — Mean unsigned angular distance (degrees) between the allocation circular mean and the actual outcome: \frac{1}{|\mathcal{O}|} \sum_{t \in \mathcal{O}} |\angle(\omega_t - \bar{\phi}_t^g)|, where \mathcal{O} is the set of outcome trials and \bar{\phi}_t^g is the circular mean of \mathbf{g}_t.

9. std_angular_error — Standard deviation of per-trial angular errors.

10. mean_defense_rate — Fraction of outcome trials where the attacked slot has \geq 1 net: \frac{1}{|\mathcal{O}|} \sum_{t \in \mathcal{O}} \mathbb{I}[g_{t, s(\omega_t)} > 0], where s(\omega) = \text{round}(\omega \cdot S / 2\pi) \mod S.

11. defense_rate_improvement — Defense rate in the last 3 episodes minus the first 3 episodes.

12. mean_tracking_error — Mean angular distance (degrees) between the allocation center on trial t and the previous outcome \omega_{t-1}. Measures how closely the agent tracks the most recent observation.

13. oddball_entropy_spike — Mean entropy on trial t+1 after an oddball, minus mean entropy on regular trials.

14. oddball_angular_shift — Mean angular shift (degrees) of allocation center from trial t-1 to t+1 around oddball trials.

15. oddball_angular_shift_regular — Same metric computed around non-oddball outcome trials (baseline).

16. oddball_shift_ratio — Feature 14 divided by Feature 15. Values > 1 indicate the agent reacts more strongly to oddballs than to regular outcomes.

17. oddball_recovery_speed — Mean angular distance of allocation center on trials t+1, t+2, t+3 from the pre-oddball position (t-1), averaged across oddballs.

18. frac_oddball_followed — Fraction of oddballs where the allocation on t+1 is closer to the oddball direction \omega_t than the allocation on t-1 was.

19–21. transition_angular_error_t1/t3/t5 — Mean angular error on trials 1, 3, and 5 after episode transitions (z-state switches).

22. transition_recovery_slope — Linear regression slope of angular error over trials 1–5 after transitions. Negative slope = error decreasing = fast recovery.

23. transition_entropy_peak — Maximum entropy in the first 3 post-transition trials.

24. transition_entropy_recovery — Number of trials until entropy returns to baseline (\leq \bar{H} + 0.5 \cdot \text{SD}(H)) after a transition.

25. mean_angular_error_late_episode — Mean angular error on trials 6+ within each episode (baseline accuracy after initial learning).

26. transition_recovery_improvement — Linear slope of recovery speeds across the 8 transitions. Positive = recovery gets faster over the session (meta-learning).

27. cue_offset_learned — Mean angular offset (degrees) between allocation centers for Cue A vs. Cue B, computed per episode and averaged. True value: 70°.

28. cue_offset_std — Standard deviation of per-episode cue offsets.

29. cue_defense_rate_diff — Mean absolute difference in defense rate between Cue A and Cue B trials, per episode.

30. cue_entropy_diff — Mean absolute difference in entropy between Cue A and Cue B trials, per episode.

31. mean_trial_shift — Mean angular shift (degrees) of allocation center between consecutive trials.

32. std_trial_shift — Standard deviation of trial-to-trial shifts.

33. frac_large_shifts — Fraction of consecutive trial pairs with > 45° shift (proxy for perceived state switches).

34. autocorr_lag1 — Circular autocorrelation at lag 1: \frac{1}{T-1} \sum_t \cos(\bar{\phi}_{t+1}^g - \bar{\phi}_t^g). High values = stable allocation direction.

35. autocorr_lag3 — Same at lag 3 (captures stability across cue alternations).

36. omission_entropy_change — Mean entropy change from trial t-1 to t+1 around omission trials.

37. omission_shift — Mean angular shift of allocation center from t-1 to t+1 around omissions. Should be near zero for a normative agent (no information received on omission trials).

38. defense_rate_slope — Linear regression slope of per-episode defense rate over the 9 episodes.

39. angular_error_slope — Linear regression slope of per-episode angular error.

40. odd_even_episode_diff — Absolute difference in defense rate between odd-numbered and even-numbered episodes. Captures asymmetry in learning across alternating episodes.

records.content:
47. oddball_persistence — Mean angular distance (degrees) maintained from the nominal state across the post-oddball trials, averaged over oddballs.

48. spontaneous_switch_rate — Rate of large allocation jumps (>45°) that are not preceded by an oddball, i.e. false-alarm switching.

Captures large, structured jumps; this is the feature most sensitive to the structured template-inference jumps the agent deliberately does not model, and is the hardest residual in posterior-predictive checks.

This is the direct behavioural marker for placement_noise: it isolates undirected, memoryless placement scatter from structured inference. It increases monotonically with placement_noise (≈ 17° at placement_noise = 0 to ≈ 42° at the prior upper bound).

records.content:
This section documents the identifiability analysis of the perceived-volatility
parameter h_switch, the rationale for its prior bound, and the relationship
between h_switch and noise_reactivity observed in the participant data. The
analysis is fully reproducible via h_switch_grid.py.

hierarchy.lvl1: h_switch Identifiability and the noise_reactivity Coupling
h_switch Identifiability and the noise_reactivity Coupling

records.content:
In an initial fit with the h_switch prior extended to [0.005, 0.35], a large
share of participants had posteriors pressed against the upper bound: 59% had
their 97.5% credible limit pinned at 0.35, and 68% had posterior means above
0.30. Taken at face value this would imply that most participants believe the
latent state switches on roughly every third trial — far more often than the
true switch rate (~0.05 per trial; episodes are 16–24 trials long). This was
implausible on its face and motivated a systematic investigation rather than
simply accepting the values or extending the bound further.

hierarchy.lvl1: h_switch Identifiability and the noise_reactivity Coupling
hierarchy.lvl2: The switch mechanism and why behaviour saturates

hierarchy.lvl1: h_switch Identifiability and the noise_reactivity Coupling
hierarchy.lvl2: The switch mechanism and why behaviour saturates

records.content:
In the v2 agent, a single oddball produces an outcome at the other latent
state’s location (the oddball displacement of +120° coincides with the
alternative state). Working through the Bayesian belief update with a
freshly-committed prior, the raw posterior over the alternative state crosses
0.5 — i.e. the agent commits to a full state switch — exactly whenh_{\text{switch}} > \rho_{\text{eff}} = \rho_{\text{fixed}} \cdot \text{noise\_reactivity},

with \rho_{\text{fixed}} = 0.10. This is the Piray & Daw (2021)
volatility-versus-stochasticity trade-off emerging directly from the mixture
likelihood: whether a surprising outcome is attributed to a changed rule
(volatility, h_switch) or to noise (stochasticity, noise_reactivity).

The crucial consequence is that the switching behaviour is governed by whether
the agent is above or below this threshold, not by the precise value of
h_switch. Once h_switch exceeds 0.1 · noise_reactivity, the agent switches
at essentially every oddball, and there are no further switching opportunities
to exploit. Behaviour therefore saturates: higher h_switch values become
behaviourally indistinguishable.



Figure 1:Switch-interpretation behaviour (oddball_follow_switch) as a function of
h_switch at four noise_reactivity levels. Each curve rises sharply at its
own threshold h = 0.1 \cdot nr (dotted vertical lines) and then plateaus.
Above threshold, behaviour is flat — h_switch is no longer identifiable from
behaviour. The highest informative region is reached at h \approx 0.30, the
threshold for the largest noise_reactivity in the prior (nr = 3.0).

Because noise_reactivity ranges up to 3.0, the largest informative value of
h_switch is approximately 0.10 \cdot 3.0 = 0.30. Beyond this, no
noise_reactivity value leaves the behaviour unsaturated, so additional prior
mass above 0.30 contributes only non-identifiable parameter space — precisely
the region that produces the ceiling artefact.

principled criterion is the saturation analysis, not the raw correlation. Both
converge on the same conclusion.

Decision: the h_switch prior upper bound is set to 0.30, the point at
which the switch threshold for the maximum noise_reactivity is reached. This
is the largest bound for which the entire prior remains behaviourally
identifiable, and it avoids the implausible near-ceiling values while preserving
the joint recovery of h_switch and noise_reactivity.

hierarchy.lvl1: h_switch Identifiability and the noise_reactivity Coupling
hierarchy.lvl2: The h_switch–noise_reactivity coupling is genuine, not an artefact

records.content:
Across participants, posterior h_switch and noise_reactivity are positively
correlated (r = +0.60). This is theoretically expected: a person who perceives
the environment as more volatile (high h_switch) and simultaneously attributes
surprising outcomes more readily to genuine change rather than noise is
expressing a coherent, correlated cognitive style. Because the two parameters
sit on either side of the same switch threshold, a positive association across
individuals is exactly what the volatility/stochasticity framework predicts.

A coupling of this kind could, in principle, also arise as an inference
artefact — if the network compressed the two parameters along the threshold
line. We tested this directly. In simulation, noise_reactivity and h_switch
were drawn independently; if the inference induced a spurious coupling, the
estimated parameters would correlate despite the independent ground truth.
They do not: the estimated correlation is ≈ 0 (and slightly negative), while the
real-participant correlation is strongly positive.



Figure 3:Left: simulated data with noise_reactivity and h_switch drawn
independently. The estimated parameters show no spurious correlation
(estimated r ≈ 0), confirming the inference does not manufacture coupling.
Right: real participants. The posteriors show a clear positive coupling
(r = +0.60), and all participants lie above the single-oddball switch threshold
h = 0.1 \cdot nr (dashed line) — i.e. they reliably treat oddballs as state
switches. The coupling is therefore a genuine psychological effect.

Because the simulated check rules out an inference-induced artefact, the
correlation observed in the real data reflects genuine individual differences in
cognitive style. This is a substantive finding rather than a nuisance, and it is
consistent with the prior theoretical expectation that perceived volatility and
the propensity to attribute change (rather than noise) covary.

h_switch Identifiability and the noise_reactivity Coupling

records.content:
All 34 participants lie above the single-oddball switch threshold
h_{\text{switch}} > 0.10 \cdot \text{noise\_reactivity}. The model therefore
infers that every participant reliably interprets oddballs as state switches —
consistent with the originally observed posterior-predictive behaviour, in which
participants made sharp, full-magnitude allocation jumps following oddballs. The
participants pressed toward the (previous) ceiling are specifically those with
high noise_reactivity: to reproduce their observed switch behaviour at high
noise_reactivity, the model requires a correspondingly high h_switch to keep
them above the threshold. This is the mechanistic origin of the coupling and of
the former ceiling.

records.content:
h_switch is well identified up to the switch threshold; above it,
behaviour saturates and the parameter is only weakly constrained from above.
The bound of 0.30 keeps the prior within the identifiable range.

The high h_switch values seen with the 0.35 bound should not be read as
evidence that participants believe in literally frequent latent-state
switching. They indicate that the participant sits above the switch threshold;
the precise value above threshold is not behaviourally determined.

The positive h_switch–noise_reactivity correlation is a genuine,
artefact-free psychological effect and can be reported as such, with the
simulated independence check as supporting evidence.

For downstream individual-difference analyses, the behaviourally robust
quantity is whether and how strongly a participant treats oddballs as
switches (captured by the switch-interpretation behaviour and the joint
position in the noise_reactivity–h_switch plane), interpreted together
rather than as two fully independent dimensions.

hierarchy.lvl1: Overview Computational Modeling: Amortized Bayesian Parameter Estimation
Overview Computational Modeling: Amortized Bayesian Parameter Estimation

records.content:
This chapter describes the computational modeling pipeline used to estimate participant-specific cognitive parameters from behavioral data. A short, self-contained tour of the model is given in Modeling at a Glance, and all symbols, priors and fixed constants are collected in Notation, Priors and Fixed Constants. The pipeline combines four components:

The inference agent, a parametric belief-update model with six free parameters (precision weighting, noise reactivity, belief momentum, perceived volatility, cue sensitivity, placement noise) that maps these parameters to observable behavior. It is implemented in reduced_agent_v3.py.

A feature extraction module, the deterministic extraction of 54 behavioral summary statistics from the net allocations of a session, computed by the same code for simulated and observed sessions.

An amortized model comparison, a neural classifier that assigns each participant posterior probabilities over five candidate models, from random allocation to full latent-state inference. It identifies participants whose behavior is indistinguishable from random allocation and participants who do not perform latent-state inference.

An amortized Bayesian inference network, a neural density estimator (BayesFlow) that inverts the agent model, mapping the 54 observed behavioral features to a posterior distribution over the six parameters.

The key advantage of this methodological approach is that inference is amortized. Specificially, a neural network is trained once on a large corpus of simulated agent–environment interactions, after which posterior estimation for any real participant takes approximately 3 seconds. The likelihood of the agent is defined only through its simulator and cannot be evaluated in closed form, so that sampling-based methods that require the likelihood are not available, and amortized simulation-based inference provides full posterior distributions from forward simulations alone.

Whether the resulting posteriors can be trusted is addressed in three places. Calibration and parameter recovery of the inference network on simulated data are reported in Amortized Bayesian Inference. The agreement between the fitted agent and participants’ behavior is reported in Posterior Predictive Checks. The two parameters with limited identifiability are examined in Oddball-Response Diagnostics (noise reactivity) and h_switch Identifiability (perceived volatility).

The particle-filter simulation models documented in the section The Simulation Models are not part of this pipeline and are no longer used for parameter inference.

Further information about Amortized Bayesian Inference and BayesFlow 2.0 can be found in 

Radev et al. (2020), 

Radev et al. (2023) and on the 

BayesFlow website.

hierarchy.lvl1: Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task
Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task

records.content:
Participants in the TAMBI mosquito defense task face a complex learning problem: they must infer hidden environmental regularities (latent state transitions, cue-dependent directional offsets, and the distinction between noise and genuine change) from noisy, intermittent outcome feedback. Not all participants approach this problem in the same way. Some may engage in latent structure inference, tracking hidden states and attributing surprises to their appropriate sources. Others may rely on simpler strategies: following the most recent outcome direction, learning the association between cue colours and attack directions without ever building a model of the latent state dynamics, or covering all structured attack locations without inferring which state is currently active. A small number may not engage meaningfully at all.

Before we can interpret the cognitive parameters estimated by our inference agent (

Amortized Bayesian Inference), we need to establish which type of learning strategy each participant is using. This is essential for three reasons:

Validity of parameter estimates. The six parameters of the inference agent (precision weighting, noise reactivity, belief momentum, perceived volatility, cue sensitivity, placement noise) are defined within a latent-structure-learning agent. Estimating these parameters for a participant who is not performing structure learning would be scientifically inappropriate (analogous to fitting a linear regression model to non-linear data).

Participant exclusion. Participants who clicked randomly or without meaningful engagement should be identified and excluded from subsequent analyses. Here, model comparison provides an objective, data-driven exclusion criterion.

Characterisation of the learning strategy spectrum. The distribution of winning models across participants provides insight into the prevalence of different learning strategies in the sample, and can be related to instruction condition and trait-level measures.

hierarchy.lvl1: Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task
Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task

records.content:
We employ BayesFlow’s ModelComparisonApproximator (Radev et al., 2023; Schmitt et al., 2023) to perform amortized Bayesian model comparison. The approach follows the same simulation-based inference logic as the parameter estimation pipeline: a neural classifier is trained on a large corpus of simulated behavioral data (generated from all candidate models), and then applied to real participant data to estimate posterior model probabilities.

Compared with model comparison by information criteria or by Bayes factors obtained with bridge sampling, both of which require a tractable likelihood that the present simulators do not have, amortized model comparison:

Operates on the same 54 behavioral summary features used for parameter estimation (ensuring consistency)

Returns posterior probabilities over models, whose calibration can be checked on simulated data

Requires no per-participant optimization or sampling at inference time

Can be validated via confusion matrices, calibration curves, and model recovery analyses before application to real data

The posterior model probabilities are conditional on the candidate set and on the prior over each model’s parameters. They state which of the five candidate models best accounts for a participant’s feature vector, and they do not state that this model describes the participant well in absolute terms. That question is addressed by the 

Posterior Predictive Checks.

hierarchy.lvl1: Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task
Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task

records.content:
Rather than comparing a large number of models that differ in subtle ways, we define a compact set of five models that span the qualitative spectrum from disengaged behavior to full latent structure inference. Each successive model adds a qualitatively distinct cognitive capability.



Figure 1:The candidate models. (The figure shows the original four-model set and has to be regenerated to include M_STRUCT4.)

Model

Strategy

Free parameters

M_RANDOM

Uniform random allocation

0

M_TRACK_SIMPLE

Tracks one direction, no cue differentiation, no latent states

2

M_TRACK_CUE

Tracks one direction per cue via a learned cue offset, no latent states

2

M_STRUCT4

Knows both attack directions of each cue and covers both permanently, without inferring the active state

2

M_STRUCT

Infers the active latent state and commits to it

6

The rationale for limiting the set to these models is twofold. First, the cognitive transitions (no learning → outcome tracking → cue association → knowledge of the four structured locations → state inference) capture the most important qualitative distinctions in learning strategy. Second, model variants that differ only in continuous parameter settings within the structure-learning agent (e.g. with or without oddball attribution, with fixed or free volatility) are better handled by the parameter estimation pipeline, where these differences manifest as different parameter values rather than as discrete model classes. Maintaining them as separate models would test the same cognitive dimension at both the model and the parameter level.

M_STRUCT4 was added to the original four-model set to separate two things that M_STRUCT combines, namely knowing that each cue has two possible attack directions and inferring which of the two is currently valid. A participant who has learned the four locations but hedges between the two directions of the current cue on every trial has acquired the structure of the task without performing latent-state inference, and should not be classified as M_STRUCT.

records.content:
Purpose: Tests whether behavior can be explained by exponential moving average (EMA) tracking of the most recent outcome direction, without any cue differentiation or latent state inference.

Mechanism: The agent maintains a single direction estimate \hat{\mu}, initialised at the first observed outcome and updated after each observed outcome \omega_t via a circular EMA:\hat{\mu} \leftarrow \left(\hat{\mu} + \alpha \cdot \angle(\omega_t - \hat{\mu})\right) \mod 2\pi

where \alpha is the learning rate and \angle(\cdot) denotes the signed angular distance in [-\pi, \pi]. The agent does not distinguish between cue colours: outcomes from both cues update the same direction estimate. No update occurs on omission trials.

Free parameters:

Parameter

Prior

Description

precision_weighting

\text{Uniform}(0.1, 5.0)

Controls allocation concentration (same role as in M_STRUCT)

\alpha

\text{Uniform}(0.01, 0.5)

EMA learning rate

What this model cannot capture: Cue-specific behaviour, latent state transitions, or oddball attribution.

hierarchy.lvl1: Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task
Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task

records.content:
Purpose: Tests whether behaviour can be explained by trial-by-trial tracking with a learned cue-colour association. This is a form of associative learning that does not require inferring hidden states.

Mechanism: Identical to M_TRACK_SIMPLE, with the addition of a cue-specific angular offset \hat{\delta}_B (initialised at 0) that is learned online. The prediction for Cue A is \hat{\mu}_A and for Cue B (\hat{\mu}_A + \hat{\delta}_B) \mod 2\pi. When a Cue B outcome is observed, the offset and the base direction share the prediction error:\hat{\delta}_B \leftarrow (\hat{\delta}_B + \alpha \cdot 0.3 \cdot \text{PE}_B) \mod 2\pi\hat{\mu}_A \leftarrow (\hat{\mu}_A + \alpha \cdot 0.7 \cdot \text{PE}_B) \mod 2\pi

where \text{PE}_B = \angle(\omega_t - [\hat{\mu}_A + \hat{\delta}_B]).

Free parameters: Same as M_TRACK_SIMPLE (precision_weighting, \alpha). The offset \hat{\delta}_B is a learned internal state, not a parameter with a prior.

What this model cannot capture: Latent state transitions (the agent has no concept of alternating hidden states), oddball attribution (all surprises are treated as signal), or the coexistence of two directions per cue.

hierarchy.lvl1: Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task
hierarchy.lvl3: 2.4 M_STRUCT4: Four-Location Coverage Without State Inference

records.content:
Purpose: Tests whether behaviour reflects knowledge of the four structured attack locations (two cues × two latent states) without inference about which latent state is currently active.

Mechanism: For each cue, the agent maintains up to two direction modes by circular online k-means. An observed outcome is assigned to the nearest existing mode of its cue and moves that mode toward the outcome at rate \alpha,m_j \leftarrow \left(m_j + \alpha \cdot \angle(\omega_t - m_j)\right) \mod 2\pi .

If the outcome lies more than 50° from every existing mode of that cue and fewer than two modes exist, it creates a second mode at its own location instead. On each trial, the predictive distribution is an equally weighted von Mises mixture over the available modes of the current cue (uniform over the 32 slots before the first outcome of that cue), without a state belief and without temporal weighting. The agent therefore covers both directions of the current cue on every trial and never commits to one of them.

Free parameters:

Parameter

Prior

Description

precision_weighting

\text{Uniform}(0.1, 5.0)

Controls allocation concentration

\alpha

\text{Uniform}(0.01, 0.5)

Learning rate of the direction modes

The separation threshold for creating a second mode is fixed at 50°.

What this model adds over M_TRACK_CUE: The simultaneous representation of two attack directions per cue. Because an oddball outcome lands on the other state’s direction, the second mode can also be created by an oddball.

What this model cannot capture: Commitment to one latent state, the change of that commitment at a transition, and the attribution of a displaced outcome to noise versus a change of state.

Mechanism: The six-parameter inference agent described in The Inference Agent and implemented in reduced_agent_v3.py. It implements a two-state hidden Markov model with cue-dependent offsets, an oddball mixture observation model, belief momentum, and placement noise. model_zoo_v3.py imports its parameter list and priors directly from reduced_agent_v3.py, so that the model comparison and the parameter estimation always use the same agent.

Free parameters: precision_weighting, noise_reactivity, belief_momentum, h_switch, cue_sensitivity, placement_noise (6 parameters in total).

The last capability row is not part of the intended ablation. M_TRACK_SIMPLE, M_TRACK_CUE and M_STRUCT4 place their nets deterministically given their beliefs, whereas M_STRUCT is the only directed model with undirected trial-to-trial placement scatter. Participants show substantial within-state placement scatter (see 

Posterior Predictive Checks). A classifier can therefore separate M_STRUCT from the three simpler directed models on the basis of placement scatter alone, independently of latent-state inference, and the same holds for cue_sensitivity, which only M_STRUCT has. Until the simpler models are given the same placement-noise parameter and the comparison is repeated, a classification as M_STRUCT cannot be attributed to latent-state inference specifically. records.content:
All five models produce integer net allocations \mathbf{g}_t \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{32} on every trial. These allocations are processed through the same 54-feature extraction pipeline used for parameter estimation (see the 

Feature Extraction chapter). This ensures:

Identical processing of simulated and observed data: The classifier sees the same feature representation for training (simulated data from all five models) and inference (real participant data).

Consistency with parameter estimation: A participant classified as M_STRUCT by the model comparison has their parameter estimates computed from the same features.

Interpretability: The features that drive classification can be inspected directly.

Identical processing does not guarantee that the feature vectors of real participants lie within the region of feature space covered by the simulations. Whether they do is a separate check (see Section 5.6).
