1.5 Statistical Analysis
Statistical analyses were conducted in Python (version) and R/RStudio (version).
Trial- and episode-level data were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models (LMM) fitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML) in lme4 and lmerTest, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Proportions (beta distribution) and binary outcomes (binomial distribution) were modelled with generalized linear mixed models in glmmTMB (ref), tested with Wald z-tests. Model terms are reported as Type III F-tests.
Instruction condition was entered in every model as an unordered factor with two orthogonal, sum-to-zero planned contrasts. The first compares participants told the structure with those not told it (C3 versus the mean of C1 and C2, weights −1/3, −1/3, 2/3); the second compares participants told that rules exist with those told nothing (C2 versus C1, weights −1/2, 1/2, 0). With this coding, all other terms of a model are evaluated as the unweighted mean over the three conditions. Condition differences are reported as contrasts of the estimated marginal means (emmeans package in RStudio; ref), which average over the covariates of a model. Model coefficients are reported instead for interactions of condition with trial-level predictors, where they equal the difference between the contrasted conditions in the effect of that predictor. Planned contrasts are reported unadjusted. All pairwise condition comparisons are reported with Holm correction.
Random effects followed the design of each model, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes for the within-participant predictors and, where events or episodes were nested within participants, random intercepts for these units. Where this structure produced a singular fit, it was reduced stepwise, first by removing the correlations between random effects and then by removing random slopes. The structure used is reported with each model.
For each model, pre-specified ‘main-interest’ terms (A and D, the questionnaire term of the across-condition form and the condition × questionnaire term of the moderation form; B, the event type × placement × questionnaire term and its interaction with condition; C, the questionnaire × prediction error, questionnaire × state error and condition × questionnaire × state error terms) were corrected for the five questionnaires with the Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery rate (FDR), separately for each term, and are reported as q. Simple slopes and planned contrasts derived from a model are reported unadjusted. All p-values are two-sided.
1.5.1. The Effect of the Level of Instruction on Task Behavior
The effects of instruction condition on net placement behavior were estimated with six models:
To examine how … / the effect of instruction condition on the net placement error relative to the hidden-state target, we estimated the model (M1):
log(|error| + 1) ∼ condition × (within-episode position + episode index) + cue + oddball on the preceding trial × condition + episode length + (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode),
which was fitted at trial level. Because oddball trials … they were excluded from this model (t+1), such that the error describes …  The model contained a random intercept for participant, random slopes for within-episode position and episode index, as well as a random intercept for episode within participant.
To examine the degree to which participants stacked multiple nets in a single location or distributed them across multiple locations within a trial, we estimated the circular variance (cv) of the (up to) 7 net positions as cv = 1 - R (cv {element} [0,1]), where R is the resultant length. The effect of instruction condition on circular variance of net positions per trial was modelled with a beta generalzed linear mixed model with logit link (M2):
beta(|error| + 1) ∼ condition × (within-episode position + episode index) + episode length + episode index + (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode),
which was fitted at trial level.
A beta mixed effects model was chosen because circular variance, the dependent variable, is a …..
Furthermore, we examined the magnitude of change of the placement centre from one trial to the next, and how this is modulated by instruction condition, the different types of event trials (oddballs, episode transitions and outcome omissions). The change of the placement centre (shift) was calculated as the circular distance between the cue-offset-corrected placement centres of consecutive trials. A constant of 0.001 was added to the shift estimate to prevent zeros. The model (M3):
log(shift + 0.001) ∼ condition + oddball + transition + omission on the preceding trial + condition × (oddball + transition) + within-episode position + episode index + number of oddballs so far in the episode + episode length + (1 + oddball + transition | participant) + (1 | participant:episode).
… the model comprises fixed effects of instruction condition and each event type, as well as an oddball–transition contrast per condition to examine whether the differential reactivity to oddball events versus the differential reactivity to episode transitions varies across conditions. Regular trials are the reference category.
Next, we examined whether participants transfer an episode transition shift observed in one cue to the second cue in the first trial in which the second cue occurs in the respective episode. This cross-cue transfer  was operationalized as the angular distance between two placements for the cue shown second in a new episode (|I_e|): its actual placement at its first appearance, and the placement expected had its previous placement been rotated by the episode’s 120° shift. The previous placement is the circular mean of the last three placements for that cue in the preceding episode, and |I_e| = 0° indicates complete transfer. The model (M4):
|I_e| ∼ condition × (episode index + transition direction) + number of trials of the first cue before the first trial of the second cue + (1 + episode index + that number | participant)
included … fixed effects … interaction contrasts … random effects … random slopes … and was fitted at episode level, with one estimate per episode and participant.
To examine how overall mosquito defense performance differed between instruction conditions and across the session, we fitted a binomial mixed model of whether a net intercepted the mosquito attack (M5):
intercepted ∼ condition × episode index + within-episode position + episode length + (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode).
… fixed effect of the level of instruction (condition), episode index, as well as their interaction, to test whether how mosquito defense performance varies across episodes differs between instruction conditions.   … random effects … random slopes …
The net placement error relative to the true hidden target at t0 to t+3 was modelled separately for episode transitions and oddballs, to investigate differences in net placement error patterns around the different events. An interaction effect between condition and trial (t0:t+3) operationalized how net placement error patterns around events differed across instruction conditions. The model (M6) was fitted as:
log(|error| + 1) ∼ condition × trial + (1 | participant) + (1 | participant:event),
with trial as a four-level factor (t0:t+3). Planned contrasts between conditions were computed at each placement.
Finally, we examined the effect of the level of instruction on the relative weighting of state error relative to outcome noise in trial-by-trial updating of mosquito net allocation centers. On each regular trial with an observed attack, the prediction error (observed mosquito attack direction – net placement centre) is the sum of two components known to the experimenter: the outcome noise (observed mosquito attack direction – hidden-state target) and the state error (hidden-state target – net placement centre). The change of the net placement centre from that trial to the next was modelled as (M7):
update ∼ condition × (prediction error + state error) + next-trial cue switch × (prediction error + state error) + (1 + prediction error + state error | participant).
In this parameterization, the coefficient of the prediction error is the weight on outcome noise, i.e. on the irreducible stochasticity, and thus the irreducible component of the total uncertainty. The coefficient of the state error is the additional weight on state error (distance of the net placement to the hidden-state target) beyond the weight on noise; the estimate is zero for a learner that responds to every outcome alike. All angles were expressed in the participant’s own frame (after removing the learned cue offset), and pairs in which the next trial showed either cue were included. Condition-specific additional weights were obtained as simple slopes with emtrends (ref), at pairs in which the next trial showed the same cue.
1.5.2 Models of the Questionnaire Score Associations
To examine how internalizing symptoms modulate overall task performance and signatures of structural inference, we estimated four linear mixed-effects-models (A–D) per questionnaire scale (trait anxiety [STICSA-T], state anxiety STICSA-S], depressive symptoms [BDI-II], intolerance of uncertainty [UI-18] and obsessive compulsive behavior [OCI-R]). Model A asks whether questionnaire scores relate to overall performance, as a boundary condition for the remaining models. Model B asks whether questionnaire scores relate to the response to an episode transition differently than to an oddball, that is, to a displaced attack that does or does not signal a change of latent state. Model C asks whether questionnaire scores relate to the weighting of state error (i.e. angular error between the participant’s current placement and the hidden target angle) relative to outcome noise. Model D asks whether questionnaire scores relate to the transfer of an episode transition to the second (i.e. previously unseen within the new episode) color cue. Each model was fitted separately for each of the five questionnaires.
Each model was fitted in two forms. First, we fitted the models across instruction conditions, with the model containing the questionnaire but no condition × questionnaire interaction, so that the questionnaire slope is estimated from all participants, each condition contributing in proportion to its size. These models are estimated to examine whether a questionnaire is associated with the outcome irrespective of instruction (i.e. which information about the hidden structure was provided). Second, we fitted an extended form of this model, by adding the condition × questionnaire interactions. From these models, the questionnaire slopes were estimated in each condition, pooled over C1 and C2 (participants not told the structure), and as the two planned contrasts between conditions. In these moderation-form models, the questionnaire main effect is the unweighted mean of the three condition-specific slopes, in which the (current) 13 C3 participants count as much as the (current) 29 C2 participants, and it is therefore not used as the across-condition estimate.
To examine whether questionnaire scores are associated with overall task performance (Model A), we extended  M1 and M5 by the questionnaire (A1, error relative to the hidden-state target, A2, interception), with the questionnaire term added to the fixed effects of M1 and M5 and the same random effects (A1, A2, (1 + within-episode position + episode index | participant) + (1 | participant:episode)).
Whether questionnaire scores are related to differences in response to oddballs compared to episode transitions was examined across the first (t+1) and second (t+2) post-event trial. For each episode transition and each oddball, the net placements in  t+1 and t+2 entered the model,
outcome ∼ condition × event type × trial × questionnaire + (1 + event type | participant) + (1 | participant:event),
with event type (oddball, transition) and placement (t+1, t+2) coded −1/2 and +1/2. The outcome was net placement error relative to the hidden-state target (B1) or net entropy (B2). The three-way interaction event type × trial × questionnaire tests whether the association of the questionnaire with the change of the outcome from t+1 to t+2 differs between episode transitions and oddballs. From the model, the questionnaire slope was estimated for each event type and placement, together with its change from t+1 to t+2 for each event type and the difference between event types at each placement.
In B2, the random slope for event type produced a singular fit and was removed. Because the three-way interaction term varies within participants, B1 was refitted as a sensitivity model with uncorrelated by-participant random slopes for event type, trial and their interaction (reduced to event type and event type × trial where singular). For B2, these random slopes were estimated at zero, so that the sensitivity model reproduced the primary model. MOVE THIS PARAGRAPH TO RESULTS?
Furthermore, we examined whether questionnaire scores modulated the relative weighting of state error (net placement error relative to the hidden state target) relative to outcome noise in trial-by-trial updating of mosquito net allocation centers, using the model (Model C)
update ∼ condition × (prediction error + state error) + questionnaire × prediction error + questionnaire × state error + condition × questionnaire × state error + next-trial cue switch × (prediction error + state error) + (1 | participant).
The questionnaire × prediction error term operationalized the effect of the questionnaire scores on the weight on outcome noise; the questionnaire × state error term operationalized the effect of questionnaire scores on the additional weight on state error. Condition-specific slopes of the additional weight on state error were computed as linear combinations of the fixed effects (lmerTest::contest). The model contains a by-participant random intercept; a sensitivity model added an uncorrelated by-participant random slope for the state error (see supplementary material, ADD).
An extended version of the cross-cue transfer model (M4) described above to examine whether questionnaire scores differentially modulated cross-cue transfer across instruction conditions. The model was estimated (Model D) as
|I_e| ∼ condition × questionnaire + number of first-cue trials × questionnaire + condition × (episode index + transition direction) + (1 + episode index + number of first-cue trials || participant),
with the number of first-cue trials centred on its mean. The random-effect correlations were removed because the correlated structure was singular. The interaction between the number of first-cue trials after an episode transition and questionnaire score additionally tested whether questionnaire scores are associated with differences in cross-cue transfer for different numbers of consecutive observations of the first color cue after an episode transition. To assess the influence of single participants on the slope in C3, the moderation form was refitted leaving out each of the 13 C3 participants with questionnaire data in turn. The increase of error on the trial after an oddball was significantly larger in C3 than in C1 and C2 (condition × oddball on the preceding trial coefficient = 0.37 log units, SE = 0.093, t(10640) = 4.02, p < .001).

Participant-level mean net placement error on stable regular trials was 53.6° in C1, 47.1° in C2 and 19.4° in C3.



Figure 1:Estimated marginal means of the log absolute error by condition as estimated with M1.

The effect of instruction on how many mosquitos were intercepted (proportion) was estimated with a binomial mixed-effects model (M4) of …. . Mosquito attack interception depends jointly on the position of the nets, their spread and chance, so the defense rate is treated here as a summary measure of task performance.

records.content:
The condition effects (level of instruction) on net placement error relative to the target angle (hidden-state target) after events was estimated with a linear mixed-effects model (M6), as planned contrasts of the condition means at each net placement. After episode transitions, the difference between conditions depended significantly on the trial (condition × trial F(6, 1618) = 15.48, p < .001) – on the transition trial itself (t0), placed before the first attack of the new latent state, net placement error did not differ significantly between conditions (C3 versus C1 + C2, 0.16 log units, SE = 0.139, t(235.9) = 1.16, p = .247; C2 versus C1, −0.08, SE = 0.127, t(236.6) = −0.65, p = .517). From the first net placement after the episode transition onward, net placement error was significantly lower in C3 than in C1 and C2, by an amount that increased across trials.

The model-estimated mean net placement error was 3.98 (C1), 3.80 (C2) and 3.14 (C3) log units at t+1, 3.53, 3.36 and 2.39 at t+2, and 3.82, 3.63 and 2.48 at t+3. Descriptively, the net placement center at t+1 had moved 0.24 (C1), 0.29 (C2) and 0.61 (C3) of the 120° rotation toward the new latent state, and at t+2 0.34, 0.37 and 0.79. In all conditions, net placement error rose again from t+2 to t+3. This rise coincides with the first appearance of the other color cue after the episode transition, which carries higher error than a repeat appearance of the first color cue (supplementary analysis ADD).

After oddballs, the difference between conditions did not depend significantly on the trial (condition × trial F(6, 2839) = 2.08, p = .052). Net placement error was lower in C3 than in C1 and C2 in every trial, including the oddball trial itself (t0, −0.81 log units, SE = 0.172, t(96.9) = −4.72, p < .001; t+1, −0.58, p = .001; t+2, −0.91, p < .001; t+3, −0.96, p < .001), and did not differ significantly between C2 and C1 in any trial (all p ≥ .093). Because oddballs occur within stable phases, in which C3 participants were more accurate, the C3 advantage after oddballs reflects their accuracy before the oddball rather than a different response to it.

The additional weight on state error (updating based on the hidden state target) compared to weight on noise was estimated with the weighting model (M7) described above. Condition-specific weights were obtained as simple slopes, and condition differences as planned contrasts of those slopes.

The additional weight on state error did not differ significantly from zero in C1 (0.07, SE = 0.095, t(60.9) = 0.72, p = .476), and it was significantly greater than zero in C2 (0.25, SE = 0.088, t(43.2) = 2.80, p = .008) and in C3 (0.66, SE = 0.184, t(658.0) = 3.56, p < .001). It was significantly greater in C3 than in C1 and C2 (planned contrast = 0.50, SE = 0.188, t(386.3) = 2.65, p = .008), and it did not differ significantly between C2 and C1 (planned contrast = 0.18, SE = 0.118, t(41.8) = 1.52, p = .137).

The weight on outcome noise was significantly greater than zero in C1 (0.37, SE = 0.094, t(57.8) = 3.87, p < .001) and C2 (0.30, SE = 0.088, t(41.6) = 3.36, p = .002), but not in C3 (0.08, SE = 0.181, t(562.3) = 0.44, p = .663). The planned contrasts of the weight on outcome noise were not significant (C3 versus C1 + C2, −0.25, SE = 0.185, t(334.3) = −1.36, p = .176; C2 versus C1, −0.07, SE = 0.118, t(39.8) = −0.58, p = .564).



Figure 4:Note.

Expressed as percentages, participants in C1 followed on average 37% of the outcome noise and corrected 43% of the state error, participants in C2 followed 30% and corrected 54%, and participants in C3 followed 8% of the noise and corrected 73% of the state error. The weight on outcome noise thus decreased descriptively with instruction, but only the additional weight on state error differed significantly between participants told and not told the structure. Participants in C1 corrected their error about the hidden state no more than they followed outcome noise, whereas participants in C3 corrected state error selectively.

records.content:
The associations of the questionnaires with the change of mosquito net placement error from the first to the second trial after an event were estimated with Model B1. The three-way interaction of event type × trial × questionnaire, tested whether the association of a questionnaire with the change of net placement error from t+1 to t+2 differs between episode transitions and oddballs.

In the across-condition form, this interaction was significant for OCI (F(1, 1432) = 7.76, p = .005, q = .022), STICSA trait anxiety (F(1, 1416) = 6.92, p = .009, q = .022) and STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 1433) = 4.91, p = .027, q = .045), at the threshold for IU (F(1, 1422) = 3.84, p = .050, q = .063), and not significant for BDI (F(1, 1419) = 0.61, p = .435). For the two STICSA scales, the association of the questionnaire with the change of net placement error from t+1 to t+2, averaged over event types, was also significant (trial × questionnaire, STICSA state F(1, 1433) = 8.92, p = .003; STICSA trait F(1, 1416) = 8.52, p = .004).

The simple slopes of the questionnaires show where this interaction arises. After episode transitions, net placement error decreased more steeply from t+1 to t+2 with higher STICSA trait scores (change of the slope = −0.25 log units per SD, SE = 0.072, t(1358) = −3.50, p < .001), STICSA state scores (−0.24, SE = 0.072, t(1361) = −3.28, p = .001) and OCI scores (−0.17, SE = 0.072, t(1361) = −2.32, p = .021), and not significantly with IU (−0.10, p = .18) or BDI scores (−0.11, p = .15). After oddballs, the change of net placement error from t+1 to t+2 was not associated with any questionnaire (STICSA trait −0.01, STICSA state −0.03, OCI 0.09, IU 0.08, BDI −0.03, all p ≥ .12).

The steeper decrease in net placement error after episode transitions for higher STICSA trait, STICSA state and OCI scores arose from higher net placement error at t+1. On the first placement after an episode transition, higher STICSA state scores were significantly associated with higher error relative to the new target (simple slope = 0.20 log units per SD, SE = 0.074, t(103.6) = 2.76, p = .007), and descriptively, higher STICSA trait (0.14, SE = 0.075, t(102.2) = 1.89, p = .062) and OCI scores (0.14, SE = 0.075, t(103.3) = 1.91, p = .059) showed the same tendency, but without reaching significance. At t+2, none of these slopes was significant (STICSA state −0.03, STICSA trait −0.11, OCI −0.02, all p ≥ .15). At t+1, the slope after episode transitions exceeded the slope after oddballs significantly for OCI (difference = 0.19, SE = 0.083, t(114.6) = 2.30, p = .023) and at the threshold (“AT THE THRESHOLD” IS WEIRD FOR p = .058 OR AT LEAST NOT BEST PRACTISE BUT I GOT STUCK FINDING A BETTER WORDING (for now)) for STICSA state anxiety (0.16, SE = 0.083, t(114.0) = 1.91, p = .058). After oddballs, the slopes at t+1 were close to zero for all questionnaires (between −0.05 and 0.05, all p ≥ .47).

In the sensitivity form with by-participant random slopes for event type, placement and their interaction, the focal interaction remained significant for STICSA trait anxiety (F(1, 69.3) = 5.59, p = .021) and STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 69.1) = 5.19, p = .026), and was at the threshold (SEE ABOVE) for IU (F(1, 67.9) = 3.86, p = .054) and OCI (F(1, 68.9) = 3.57, p = .063).

In the moderation form, the four-way interaction (i.e. the three-way interaction described above + questionnaire as a fourth term; condition × event type × trial × questionnaire) did not depend significantly on instruction condition for any questionnaire (condition × event type × trial × questionnaire, all F(2, ≈1410) ≤ 0.81, all p ≥ .44). For STICSA trait anxiety, the difference between episode transitions and oddballs in the change of the slope from t+1 to t+2 was of the same size in C1 and C2 (−0.24, SE = 0.119, t(1416) = −2.04, p = .042) as in C3 (−0.25, SE = 0.166, t(1392) = −1.53, p = .127), and the same held for STICSA state anxiety (C1 and C2, −0.30, p = .020; C3, −0.23, p = .30) (NOTE. NOTICE THE DIFFERENCES IN P VALUES WHICH ARE LIKELY DUE TO SAMPLE SIZE DIFF. EFFECT COULD REACH SIGNIFICANCE AT (MUCH) LARGER N). For OCI, it (SPECIFY) was present in C1 and C2 (−0.25, SE = 0.101, t(1417) = −2.49, p = .013) and smaller in C3 (−0.15, p = .56), without a significant difference between them (p = .71).



Figure 5:Note.

Descriptively, the division of the nets between the two directions showed the same delay (Fig. X). On the first placement after an epsisode transition, participants in the lowest tertile of STICSA state scores already placed a larger mean share of their nets within one position of the new direction than of the old direction (0.36 versus 0.25). Participants in the highest tertile did not (0.26 versus 0.31). On the second placement, both tertiles placed 0.38–0.40 of their nets at the new direction and about 0.20 at the old direction. These values are descriptive; no statistical tests were computed on these descriptive differences.

Across individual episode transitions, about a third of net placements in the first trial after the respective episode transition (t+1) had no net at the new direction in either tertile, and net placements with all or nearly all nets at the new direction were less frequent in the highest tertile. The higher error at t+1 therefore reflects fewer nets moved (placed at?)  to the new direction, rather than a net placement at an intermediate direction.



Figure 6:Note.

Two further patterns in the moderation form were not part of the analyses based on the interaction terms (SPECIFY). First, the association of the questionnaire with the change of net placement error from t+1 to t+2 differed between conditions for OCI (condition × trial × questionnaire F(2, 1416) = 8.49, p < .001), BDI (F(2, 1410) = 5.22, p = .005) and STICSA trait anxiety (F(2, 1408) = 4.74, p = .009). These interactions were carried by the contrast between C2 and C1. In C2 relative to C1, higher scores were associated with a steeper decrease of net placement error from t+1 to t+2 after oddballs (C2 versus C1, STICSA trait −0.39, p = .008; BDI −0.37, p = .013; OCI −0.28, p = .024; STICSA state −0.33, p = .034) and, for BDI and OCI, also after episode transitions (BDI −0.41, p = .036; OCI −0.40, p = .013). Second, in C3, net placement error after oddballs increased from t+1 to t+2 with higher IU (change of the slope = 0.27 log units per SD, SE = 0.132, t(1510) = 2.07, p = .038) and OCI scores (0.32, SE = 0.157, t(1518) = 2.07, p = .039), but not with STICSA or BDI scores (all p ≥ .68).

Participants with higher STICSA and OCI scores thus placed the mosquito nets further from the new target on the first trial after an episode transition and fully closed this gap by the second trial, whereas their net placement locations (relative to the target) after an oddball did not differ. This pattern was present irrespective of instruction for the STICSA scales. Where the structure had been instructed, participants with higher IU and OCI scores moved further from the target in the placement after an oddball, consistent with their higher net placement error in C3 in Model A1.

The associations of the questionnaire scores (ACTUALLY, MAYBE “INTERNALIZING SYMPTOMS” OR SMTH LIKE THAT INSTEAD OF QUESTIONNAIRE SCORES COULD BE BETTER?) with net entropy after events were estimated with Model B2 (SPECIFY). In the across-condition form, the event type × trial × questionnaire interaction was significant for OCI (F(1, 1405) = 8.26, p = .004, q = .021), STICSA trait anxiety (F(1, 1395) = 6.10, p = .014, q = .034) and STICSA state anxiety (F(1, 1407) = 4.42, p = .036, q = .060), and not significant for IU (F(1, 1399) = 3.01, p = .083) or BDI (F(1, 1397) = 0.50, p = .48).

For STICSA trait anxiety and OCI, the interaction arose at t+1. On the first placement after an event, higher scores were associated with a wider allocation after oddballs than after episode transitions (difference of the slopes, transition minus oddball, STICSA trait −0.054 bits per SD, SE = 0.025, t(2213) = −2.21, p = .027; OCI −0.052, SE = 0.025, t(2216) = −2.12, p = .034). At t+2, this difference was absent (STICSA trait 0.006, p = .80; OCI 0.019, p = .45), because the allocation after episode transitions widened from t+1 to t+2 with higher OCI scores (change of the slope = 0.048 bits per SD, SE = 0.020, t(1357) = 2.43, p = .015) and, at the threshold, higher STICSA trait scores (0.034, SE = 0.019, t(1356) = 1.73, p = .084).
STICSA state anxiety showed a different pattern. Higher state scores were associated with a wider allocation at both placements and after both events (simple slopes between 0.10 and 0.13 bits per SD; oddball t+1, 0.13, SE = 0.048, t(66.4) = 2.72, p = .008; transition t+2, 0.13, SE = 0.050, t(78.5) = 2.64, p = .010; transition t+1, 0.10, p = .057; oddball t+2, 0.11, p = .022).

In the moderation form, the difference between oddballs and episode transitions at t+1 was present in C1 and C2 for STICSA trait anxiety (−0.098 bits per SD, SE = 0.033, t(2211) = −3.00, p = .003), OCI (−0.065, SE = 0.028, t(2212) = −2.33, p = .020) and IU (−0.056, SE = 0.027, t(2212) = −2.05, p = .040), and close to zero in C3 (STICSA trait 0.006, OCI 0.040, IU 0.046, all p ≥ .43). The planned contrast between C3 and C1 + C2 was not significant (STICSA trait 0.10, p = .066; OCI 0.10, p = .17; IU 0.10, p = .12), and the four-way interaction was not significant for any questionnaire (all p ≥ .51).

After a single displaced mosquito attack, participants with higher STICSA trait, OCI and, in C1 and C2, IU scores thus spread their nets more widely when the mosquito attack was an oddball than when it was an episode transition. After an episode transition, their allocation on the first trial after the respective epsidoe transition (t+1) was not wider than that of participants with lower scores, and it widened on the second trial (t+2). Participants with higher STICSA state scores spread their nets more widely after both kinds of event.

In the across-condition form, higher OCI and STICSA state scores were significantly associated with a lower weight on outcome noise (questionnaire × prediction error coefficient, OCI −0.091 per SD, SE = 0.028, t(8264) = −3.20, p = .001, q = .007; STICSA state −0.088, SE = 0.030, t(8267) = −2.93, p = .003, q = .009). The associations for STICSA trait anxiety (−0.047, p = .13), IU (−0.049, p = .14) and BDI (−0.038, p = .26) were in the same direction but did not reach significance.

Higher scores on four questionnaires were significantly associated with a greater additional weight on state error (questionnaire × state error coefficient, STICSA trait 0.096 per SD, SE = 0.032, t(8266) = 3.02, p = .003, q = .006; OCI 0.093, SE = 0.028, t(8252) = 3.27, p = .001, q = .005; STICSA state 0.077, SE = 0.030, t(8266) = 2.55, p = .011, q = .018; IU 0.069, SE = 0.033, t(8266) = 2.09, p = .037, q = .046). Associations with |I_e| were estimated with Model D. In the across-condition form, higher OCI scores were significantly associated with larger |I_e|, that is, with less transfer of the hidden-state change (i.e. the episode transition with it’s 120° environment shift) to the second cue (6.3° per SD, SE = 2.92, t(61.1) = 2.16, p = .035, q = .17). Descriptively, STICSA trait anxiety showed the same tendency (5.0°, SE = 2.94, t(61.3) = 1.70, p = .094), without reaching significance. STICSA state anxiety, IU and BDI were not associated with |I_e| (all p ≥ .36).

In the moderation form, the association did not depend significantly on condition for any questionnaire (condition × questionnaire, IU F(2, 59.2) = 2.29, p = .110; BDI F(2, 60.0) = 2.15, p = .125; OCI, STICSA trait and STICSA state, all p ≥ .36). In C3, the simple slope was positive for IU (13.7° per SD, SE = 6.97, t(58.9) = 1.96, p = .055) and OCI (16.9°, SE = 8.27, t(58.8) = 2.04, p = .046), and the planned contrast between C3 and C1 + C2 showed a trend for IU (14.4°, SE = 7.69, t(59.0) = 1.88, p = .065) and was not significant for OCI (12.5°, p = .16). In C1 and C2, the pooled slopes were close to zero (IU −0.8°, OCI 4.3°, both p ≥ .19). For BDI, the slope was larger in C2 than in C1 (C2 versus C1, 16.3°, SE = 7.97, t(60.0) = 2.05, p = .045), with slopes of opposite sign in the two conditions (C1 −9.3°, C2 7.0°, both p ≥ .14).

When each of the 13 C3 participants with questionnaire data was left out in turn, the C3 slope remained positive in every refit, ranging from 7.7° to 17.2° per SD for IU and from 6.6° to 23.3° for OCI. Its significance varied with the omitted participant (IU, p = .021 to .343; OCI, p = .009 to .614). (CAN BE REMOVED WITH HIGHER N)
Descriptively, |I_e| in C1 and C2 was distributed around the 90° expected for random net placement across the whole range of IU scores (Fig. 4a). In C3, participants with lower IU scores showed |I_e| of about 35°–55°, whereas participants with the highest scores showed |I_e| at or above 90°, the level of the uninstructed conditions (Fig. 4b).

Higher OCI scores were thus associated with less transfer of the change to the second cue across conditions, and higher IU and OCI scores with less transfer in C3, where the structure had been instructed. The C3 estimates rest on 13 participants and depend on individual participants (ATM).

(the following paragraph is a mediocre draft - written spontaneously and not good, but kept as a starting point)

Trait anxiety and related constructs (as well as internalizing symptoms more broadly, see below) show no significant main-effect relationship with structural inference. Nonetheless, the descriptive effects build a coherent set of condition-dependent and transition-specific associations that converge across scales and analyses. The clearest is a large, uniformly-signed family of trait x instruction-depth interactions on cue-dissociation (IU-prospective β=−0.62, ERS −0.61, IU-total −0.55, plus EAT, IU-inhibitory, OCI same-signed), suggesting that the structural-generalization benefit of deeper instruction is systematically modulated by uncertainty-/internalizing-related traits, i.e. individual differences express themselves specifically where structure is manipulated. A second group of descriptive effects links (state/cognitive) anxiety to higher net-placement entropy (and lower stacking) (β≈+0.27). Interpreted cautiously, high anxiety individuals may thus infer higher local stochasiticity compared to individuals with low-to-medium anxiety. This converges with earlier evidence from tasks in which individuals learn to distinguish between volatility and stochasticity, where high trait anxiety was assocated with an overestimation of stochasticity and an underestimation of volatility (cite). Crucially, this was commonly interpreted as reduced or even affected learning (cite). Our results provide an alternative interpretation: while outcome variability within stable latent states is more readily attributed to stochastic noise, thereby decreasing sensitivity to volatility as long as this volatility does not arise from a specific hidden structure, reactivity to structured variablility of the generative structure itself (i.e. state transitions) is increased while sensitivity to stochasiticity at this structure-level is decreased. This is not consistent with generally altered/ reduced learning but with a different focus on what should be learned. It is further consistent with evidence demonstrating, that high anxiety individuals have a higher tendency to infer and rely on (hidden) structures in the context of latent state inference (Zika et al., 2023). A higher structural prior / more pronouced expectation that dynamics are driven by switches between discrete states rather than continuous gradual dynamics would give rise to a “misatribution” of volatility to stochasticity as long as the observed variablility through volatility is not distinguishable from local within-state stochasticity (actually a higher tolerance for local noise, in order to stick with model that provides a structured explanation for the observed dynamics, thereby allowing for straightforward action selection - otherwise, the uncertainty about the model generating outcomes would have to increase rapidly). But as soon as volatility is governed by a certain hidden structure that can be identified, this “misattribution” diminishes. Instead, high-anxiety/ internalizing idividuals show a relatively “better” structural inference compared to individuals with lower anxiety/internalizing symptom load.

interpreted suggesting that high trait anxiety (or internalizing symptoms more broadly) ....
A third, smaller but convergent cluster (β≈+0.2 across SLI level, transition-recovery, and post-transition update, with the opposite sign for oddball reactivity) suggests higher internalizing goes with sharper, not weaker, structure-vs-noise dissociation - descriptively consistent with anxiety accelerating structural learning. None survive FDR at N=65 (which detects only r>=0.34), but their magnitude and cross-analysis convergence provide preliminary evidence .... .

M_SL3: STICSA-T --> transition_recovery_mean β=+0.22, p=0.079; BDI +0.22, p=0.081; STICSA-state +0.22, p=0.072. Three internalizing scales, same sign, all ~0.22

M_SL3: STICSA-T --> SLI level β=+0.22, p=0.08; OCI +0.24; IU +0.19; IU-inhibitory +0.21. Again a same-signed family around +0.2

two-stage: ERS --> rule1_marker_delta_post_transition β=+0.28, p=0.026 (largest single main effect in the whole grid)

This pattern of effects suggests that higher internalizing symptom load is associated with larger post-transition belief updates, stronger transition-recovery and a (marginally) higher structure-learning index. The sign is positive throughout, consistent with the hypothesis that anxiety may accelerate structure learning. Moreover, this pattern is specifically about transitions (genuine structural change), not about oddballs (noise). For oddballs, the direction of the effect is reversed and weaker (oddball_reactivity x IU β=−0.23, x OCI −0.29), suggesting that higher internalizing symptom load is associated with less oddball reactivity. Together, the present pattern of descriptive effects, i.e. that individuals with higher internalizing symptom load show an increased adaptivity to (hidden) structural change combined with a simultaneously reduced reactivity to oddballs (structure-level stochasticity), suggests that higher-internalizing individuals show a sharper structure-vs-noise dissociation.

Together, these results challenge the view that anxiety may affect learning. Instead they suggest that hgih anxiety individuals may have a higher sensitivity to hidden structures/ patterns that are not directly observable (obscured by noise) but carry a predictive value if inferred correctly.

records.content:
Latent-state inference is the winning account, while gradual tracking is
rejected outright. The structural model is the best-fitting model for 62 of 68
participants (91%), with a mean posterior model probability of 0.91. Both
gradual-tracking models win zero participants and have mean posterior
probability 0.00. Because the tracking models are the formal expression of the
gradual-learning alternative, this is the most direct available evidence for the RQ1
hypothesis.

The parameters are calibrated and, with one exception, well recovered.
Simulation-based calibration returns near-uniform rank histograms (rank means
467–503 of 1000 for five of six parameters). Recovery correlations are 0.996
(precision weighting), 0.985 (placement noise), 0.934 (cue sensitivity), 0.910
(belief momentum), 0.825 (perceived volatility) and 0.636 (noise reactivity).

The parameters measure what they were constructed to measure. Pre-specified
convergent-validity pairings hold for the well-recovered parameters: precision
weighting with net entropy (r = −0.87, p = 5 x 10⁻²²) and stacking (r = +0.62),
cue sensitivity with the learned cue offset (r = +0.81, p = 9 x 10⁻¹⁷), and
belief momentum with post-transition belief revision (r = −0.42, p = 4 x 10⁻⁴),
all Holm-significant within family.

Synthesis. The computational model is identifiable, calibrated and valid
against the behavioural measures it indexes, and it selects structural inference
over gradual tracking essentially unanimously.

The reason for this pattern is that the model cannot jump as fast as participants do - I’m still trying to find a solution for this but IMO even the current version captures participant behavior very well. Noise reactivity is the least identifiable parameter (recovery r = 0.64,
reliability ≈ 0.41). Diagnostic work established that this is a property of the
forward model rather than of the estimation method: an independent supervised
learner trained on the same summary features reproduces the recovery profile of
the neural estimator to two decimal places, and the parameter’s behavioural
channels are suppressed downstream (the learning gate saturates at κ = 4 with a
120° displacement, and the predictive mixture component is removed by the
commitment sharpening before net allocation). A two-stage allocation reserving
round(7 x ρ_eff) nets for the oddball location raises the ceiling from 0.60 to
0.92 in simulation, at a cost of 0.09 for perceived volatility, leaving switching
behaviour unchanged. The model has been patched and awaits retraining and
posterior predictive re-validation (just didn’t find the time yet - this is retraining No.9 (?) and the training has to run over night). Until then, results involving noise reactivity, including the absence of the predicted association with trait
anxiety, are limited by identifiability rather than evidence of absence.



Figure 17:NOTE.



Figure 3:NOTE.

Nevertheless, different noise reactivity values produce exactly the expected model behavior:



Figure 19:NOTE.

The transition-versus-oddball distinction is where the three questions come together. RQ1
establishes that instructed structure changes what is propagated across cues and
retained across trials, and that propagation scales with prior evidence. RQ3
establishes that the generative account is latent-state inference rather than
gradual tracking, and that belief momentum indexes post-transition revision. RQ2
places internalizing load on the same axis: larger post-transition updating,
lower oddball reactivity and lower belief momentum, observed consistently at the
behavioural, parameter and symptom levels, though no individual association is
resolved at the present sample size.

The three instruction conditions are the primary between-subjects manipulation in TAMBI. They vary in how much explicit structural information participants receive about the cue–direction relationships and episode transitions before the task begins.
This manipulation doesn’t just allow the comparison of learning-from-scratch with partial and complete structural knowledge, but also creates a between-condition manipulation of structural priors, representing exposure to different levels of task ambiguity.

Instruction condition is randomly assigned to each participant before the session and determines which set of instruction slides is presented by the PsychoPy script.
Three instruction conditions with different levels of Task Ambiguity, corresponding to different levels of epistemic (teal) and aleatoric (purple) uncertainty.



Figure 1:Three instruction conditions with different levels of Task Ambiguity, corresponding to different levels of epistemic (teal) and aleatoric (purple) uncertainty.

Participants learn:

The visual layout of the task (circular “arena”, 32 slots)

How to place nets (left click) and remove them (right click)

The meaning of the blood counter (performance feedback)

That mosquitoes will attack, and that placing nets in the attack direction will block them with a certain probability depending on the number of nets, stacked in the respective slot.

Participants do not learn the underlying rules of the environment:

That the two cue colors predict different directions

That a systematic angular offset exists between the two cues

That the direction pattern can change over the course of the experiment

That oddballs exist

Instruction slides:







Corresponding computational models: The pure inference models make the same assumption as Condition 1 participants — no prior structural knowledge, all structure inferred from experience.

Participants learn everything in Condition 1, plus:

That there might exist underlying rules which determine the attack direction

Participants do not learn:

That the two cue colors predict different directions

That a systematic angular offset exists between the two cues

That the direction pattern can change over the course of the experiment

That oddballs exist

Instruction slides:









Corresponding computational models: Condition 2 corresponds approximately to models that know a structure exists but must infer its parameters - most closely M3 (full Bayesian inference) and the temporal commitment models M_sticky, M_count, and M_hybrid.

Participants learn everything in Condition 2, plus:

Rule 3 (Cue Offset): The instructions explain that one color consistently predicts attacks from one angular region, while the other color consistently predicts attacks offset by approximately 70° clockwise from the first. An example illustration shows the direction pattern for both colors.

Rule 2 (Episode Rotation): The instructions explain that at irregular intervals (approximately every 20 trials), the entire direction pattern shifts by approximately 120°. Both cues shift simultaneously. The transition is not announced.

The instruction slides for Condition 3 are direction-dependent: the example illustration showing the cue–direction relationship is adapted to match the actual direction pattern in the participant’s trial schedule. This requires knowing the first occurrence of each color cue in the schedule and the corresponding attack direction, which is pre-computed from the schedule file before the session starts.

Instruction slide selection logic for the direction-dependent slide (cond_3c):first_trial_info = self.get_first_trial_directions_per_cue()
# Returns: {color: {'direction': direction_key, 'color': color_name, 'angle': angle}}

key_c = f"{info_c['direction']}_{info_c['color']}"

Available direction keys: O, R_O, R, R_U, U, L_U, L, L_O (compass directions)
Available color names: peach, curry, frog

This generates 8 \times 3 = 24 possible instruction slide variants.

Instruction slides:











Corresponding computational models: Condition 3 corresponds most closely to the rule-knowledge models: M_rule3 (knows \delta_B = 70°), M_rule2 (knows \Delta = 120°, h = 0.05), and M_rule23 (knows both).

Instruction conditions are assigned randomly with automatic balancing across conditions.

Randomization is implemented at the schedule level as well as at the condition level: participants are assigned to condition before the session begins, and the assignment is documented in the results file. Trial schedules are drawn randomly from the pre-generated pool before presenting the condition-specific (and for condition 3 also trial-schedule-specific) instruction slides.

All participants complete the same practice trial regardless of condition. The practice is a free-exploration phase with progressive hints:

If no net has been placed yet: “Try left-clicking on one of the white circles to place a net”

If one net has been placed but not multiple: “Good! Try placing more nets in different positions”

If multiple nets placed but none removed: “Now try right-clicking on a net to remove it”

When at least one net has been placed and one removed: “Perfect! [Space to continue]”

The practice arena shows the standard display but without any cue color (no actual trial is run). The participant’s placement behavior is recorded but not scored. The practice trial ends when the participant presses Space after having both placed and removed at least one net.

At the end of the session, all participants complete a questionnaire that includes a rule awareness check:

Page C (Yes/No): “Did you notice that the direction of the mosquitoes changed in a consistent way depending on the color cue that was shown?”

Page D (text input, if Yes): “How did the direction of the mosquito change depending on which color cue was shown?”

Page E (Yes/No): “Were the instructions at the beginning of the experiment clear and comprehensible?”

Page F (text input, if No): “What specifically was unclear?”

These items allow post-hoc verification of rule awareness across conditions and identification of any participants in Conditions 1 or 2 who spontaneously discovered the structural rules, or any participants in Condition 3 who failed to encode the instructions.

The screen coordinate system uses degrees of visual angle with the origin at the center of the screen. All slot positions are computed analytically from the angle formula:def angle_to_position(self, angle_deg, radius=8):
    angle_rad = math.radians(angle_deg)
    x = radius * math.cos(angle_rad)
    y = radius * math.sin(angle_rad)
    return [x, y]

The 32 slots are positioned at equal angular intervals (11.25° per slot) on the defense perimeter circle. Slot 0 is at 0° (3 o’clock position in standard math coordinates). The slot assignment for a mouse click uses nearest-slot logic:def get_slot_from_position(self, pos):
    min_distance = float('inf')
    closest_slot = None
    for i, slot_pos in enumerate(self.slot_positions):
        distance = math.sqrt((pos[0]-slot_pos[0])**2 + (pos[1]-slot_pos[1])**2)
        if distance < min_distance:
            min_distance = distance
            closest_slot = i
    return closest_slot if min_distance < 1.5 else None

The 1.5° threshold means that clicks far from all slots (e.g., near the center or outside the circle) are not registered.

Net orientation at each slot is tangential to the perimeter circle:net.ori = 90 - angle  # Rotate net to be tangent to circle

The Mosquito Defense Task is a spatial predictive inference paradigm implemented in PsychoPy. On each trial, participants allocate up to 7 defensive nets across 32 evenly spaced angular positions on a circular perimeter, with the goal of intercepting a mosquito that will subsequently attack from a direction governed by the task’s latent structure.

The task is presented with a narrative and visual framing (described in 

Gamification and Game Design) in which the participant is a defender protecting a central resource from mosquito attacks. The spatial, circular structure of the defense problem directly embodies the angular inference problem that is the scientific focus of the study.

The central visual display consists of:

A central light cue circle that changes color each trial to indicate the active cue identity. During the anticipation phase, this cue is visible; during barrier placement, it remains visible.

A defense perimeter circle on which the 32 slots are positioned at equal angular intervals (11.25° per slot).

32 slot indicators - small white circles at each slot position indicating available placement positions.

A blood counter arc - a colored arc on an inner circle indicating the current blood point total (initially 100, updated after each outcome trial).

Net visuals - image-based net stimuli that appear at slot positions when barriers are placed.

Mouse cursor - a small red circle showing the current cursor position, accompanied by a small net image and a counter showing remaining nets.

ADD: what is generated in the PsychoPy code vs what is pregenerated and imported as images
Figure 1:ADD

The Task contains nine episodes.

two latent environmental states, characterized by a 120° shift relative to each other, sequential alternating

within episodes: 2 color cues, 70° offset

~ 10% oddballs, also 120° shift in relation to the base direction (defined by the current latent environmental state and the color cue in the respective trial)



Figure 2:ADD

Each trial consists of four sequential phases:



Figure 3:ADD

The color cue appears at the center of the screen. No net placement is permitted during this phase. The cursor is centered at the start of each trial.

Purpose: The anticipation phase gives participants time to form their prediction about the attack direction and plan their net placement, without allowing pre-commitment.

Duration: Fixed at 4.0 seconds.

Eye tracking marker: ANTICIPATION_START / ANTICIPATION_END

BIOPAC marker: ANTICIPATION_START_EP{episode}

Participants use the mouse to place nets on the perimeter slots. The mouse cursor is visible and interactive during this phase.

Left click: Place one net at the nearest slot to the cursor position.

Right click: Remove one net from the slot nearest the cursor (if the slot contains at least one net).

Maximum nets: 7 per trial. Participants may place fewer; they do not need to use all 7.

Stacking: Multiple nets may be placed in the same slot, up to 7. The defense effectiveness of stacked nets follows a cubic decline function (see 

Outcomes).

Time limit: 7.0 seconds. Visual countdown is not displayed, but audio beeps sound at 3s, 2s, and 1s remaining.

Early advancement: The phase ends early if all 7 nets are placed (though participants may continue repositioning until time expires or they press no further keys).

The cursor display during placement shows: a small net image offset from the cursor, a counter displaying remaining nets (e.g., 5/7), and a hover highlight on the nearest slot.

Slot assignment uses nearest-slot logic: the clicked position maps to whichever of the 32 slots is closest. Slots are positioned at radius 8° from center; clicks anywhere on the screen are mapped to the nearest slot.

Eye tracking marker: PLACEMENT_START / PLACEMENT_END

A jittered delay between net placement and outcome delivery. The color cue remains visible. No new interactions are possible.

Duration: Drawn from a truncated exponential distribution: \text{ISI} \sim \min(\text{Exp}(\lambda = 0.5) + 2.0, 4.0) seconds.

Purpose: Prevents participants from anticipating outcome onset from a fixed delay; adds temporal jitter for physiological data analysis.

Eye tracking marker: ISI_START / ISI_END
The outcome phase varies depending on whether the current trial is an outcome trial or an omission trial.

The mosquito approaches from the attack angle, animated over 2.3 seconds. The mosquito image is selected based on the attack direction (8 directional variants: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW). The mosquito buzz sound plays throughout the animation.

Blocked outcome: If the mosquito encounters a net in its approach slot, it reverses and flies back. The show_blood_gain_feedback() function displays a green sparkle animation, “+1 ♥” rising animation, and “BLOCKED!” text. Blood points increase by 1.

Hit outcome: The mosquito reaches the center. The show_blood_loss_feedback() function displays a red flash overlay, screen shake effect, “-1 ♥” falling animation, and “BITE!” text. Blood points decrease by 1.

Hit probability is determined by the net count in the attack slot:

Nets at attack slot

This function follows a cubic decline: p_{\text{hit}}(n) = 0.5 \cdot \left(\frac{7-n}{6}\right)^3 for n > 0, with p_{\text{hit}}(0) = 1 and p_{\text{hit}}(7) = 0.

Eye tracking markers: OUTCOME_START, MOSQUITO_ANGLE_{angle}, OUTCOME_BLOCKED or OUTCOME_NOT_BLOCKED

No mosquito animation is shown. A brief “...” display appears for 2.3 seconds. No blood points change. No sound plays.

Eye tracking marker: NO_OUTCOME

Participants begin with 100 blood points. Points change by ±1 per outcome trial (no change on omission trials). The blood counter is displayed continuously as:

A numerical value at center screen

A colored arc on the inner circle that shrinks as blood points decrease

A heart symbol (♥) whose color shifts from green (>60 points) to yellow-orange (30–60) to red (<30 points)

The blood counter has no mechanical consequence in the current implementation — it does not end the experiment and does not trigger any qualitative state change. It functions purely as a continuous feedback display of cumulative performance, providing motivational salience to individual trial outcomes.

Scheduled breaks occur approximately every 40–60 trials (randomized to avoid episode boundary overlap). The break screen is displayed until the participant presses Space, after which an experimenter confirmation screen waits for the experimenter to press ‘P’ before the experiment resumes. Maximum break duration is 3 minutes. After each break, a drift correction is performed and a 3-2-1 countdown is shown before the next trial begins.

Within-task emotional state ratings are collected 1–2 times per episode. The rating is triggered at either trial 7 or trial 14 of the episode (randomly chosen per episode), but not both. If not triggered at trial 7 (50% chance), it is triggered at trial 14 by default.

The rating screen presents six continuous sliders (valence, arousal, anxiety, stress, frustration, fatigue) in randomized order. Participants drag the sliders with the mouse. The rating is confirmed by pressing Space.

Trial schedules are pre-generated as CSV files and stored in the trial_schedules/ directory. One schedule file is selected randomly at session start, ensuring that trial properties are rigorously controlled while still providing participant-level randomization. This approach avoids the risk of generating invalid schedules at runtime (e.g., constraint violations) and enables efficient session startup, ensuring low susceptibility to errors.

Each schedule file is generated by the trial_schedule_generation.ipynb notebook and encodes all trial-level information needed by the PsychoPy task: episode membership, cue color, target angle, observed angle (target + von Mises noise), outcome occurrence, and oddball flag.

This ensures controlled randomization within defined boundaries - in this way, the analysis can focus on the structural parameters of the task, while the constrained randomization (or jittering) ensures that any observed effects are not merely artifacts of a highly specific trial sequence.

Episode lengths are drawn to satisfy:

The generation procedure iteratively adjusts lengths until both constraints are satisfied. The jitter ensures that participants cannot use trial counting to predict episode transitions.

The boundary constraint is the most demanding structural requirement: the last trial of each episode and the first trial of the next episode must display the same color cue. This prevents a cue switch from co-occurring with an episode transition, ensuring that the only signal of a transition is the change in attack direction.

A secondary constraint requires that:

Episodes 2–5 each begin with 3–4 consecutive trials of the cue that initiates the learning phase

The learning-phase cue identities are balanced (2 of each identity in episodes 2–5)

All 8 episode transition cues are balanced (4 of each identity)

The planning algorithm proceeds as follows:

Generate a balanced sequence of transition cue identities (4 of identity 1, 4 of identity 2, with the first 4 balanced 2:2).

For each episode, attempt to generate a valid cue sequence satisfying:

Required start color (= last color of previous episode, if available)

Required learning-phase start color (for episodes 2–5)

Maximum within-episode color streak of 3

Approximately equal representation of both colors within the episode

If any episode produces a conflict between the boundary constraint and the learning-phase identity requirement, discard the current identity sequence and retry with a new one.

This procedure is iterated up to 1000 times. In practice, a valid plan is almost always found within ~50 attempts.

After the cue sequence is determined, outcome omission trials are assigned per episode:

Valid positions for omissions exclude:

The first 4 trials of each episode (learning phase)

The last trial of each episode

Trials immediately following a cue switch

Placement algorithm:

Compute target omission count based on a random rate drawn from [5%, 15%]

Select omission positions from valid positions, avoiding consecutive omissions where possible

If strict non-consecutive selection cannot achieve the target count, allow consecutive omissions

Oddballs are assigned after omissions, with additional constraints:

Valid positions for oddballs additionally exclude:

Trials that are already omission trials

Trials immediately adjacent (±1) to omission trials

Consecutive oddball avoidance: If the target count cannot be achieved without consecutive oddballs, the target is reduced rather than allowing consecutive oddballs.

Overlap check: A validation step confirms that no trial is simultaneously an omission and an oddball. The schedule generation notebook reports the overlap count, which must be 0.

For each trial:

The target angle is computed from:

The current episode’s base angle (= initial_start_angle for odd episodes, initial_start_angle + 120° for even episodes)

The cue identity (identity 2 adds rule3_shift = 70° to the base angle)

The actual angle is obtained by adding von Mises noise:\omega_t \sim \mathcal{VM}(\mu_{\text{target}},\, \kappa = 40)

This gives a typical angular deviation of approximately ±10° (SD ≈ 10°, range ≈ 50°, maximum range is constrained to < 60°), matching the concentration parameter used in the simulation models.

For oddball trials, the target angle is first shifted by +120°, then the same noise process is applied.

#============================================================#
# VON MISES VECTOR ENCODING FUNCTION 
#============================================================#

# function to add angle noise 
# Args:
#   - target_angle in degree
#   - noise_std in degree
#   - use_gaussian: True for gaussian noise, false for von Mises based noise
# Returns:
#   - angle with noise in degree (0-360) --> Stimulus angle

def add_angle_noise(target_angle, kappa_noise=kappa, use_gaussian=False):
        
    # Sample from von Mises distribution centred around target_angle
    target_rad = np.radians(target_angle)
    noisy_rad = vonmises.rvs(kappa_noise, loc=target_rad)
    noisy_angle = np.degrees(noisy_rad) % 360
    
    return noisy_angle

def generate_balanced_episode_lengths(n_episodes, base_length, min_length, max_length, target_mean_min, target_mean_max):
   
    target_total = base_length * n_episodes  # Target total trials
    
    while True:
        # Generate random lengths within the allowed range
        lengths = []
        for i in range(n_episodes):
            length = random.randint(min_length, max_length)
            lengths.append(length)
        
        # Check if the mean is within acceptable range
        actual_mean = sum(lengths) / n_episodes
        
        if target_mean_min <= actual_mean <= target_mean_max:
            return lengths
        
        # If mean is too low or too high, adjust some episodes
        if actual_mean < target_mean_min:
            # Need to increase some episodes
            deficit = target_total - sum(lengths)
            for i in range(min(deficit, n_episodes)):
                if lengths[i] < max_length:
                    lengths[i] += 1
        elif actual_mean > target_mean_max:
            # Need to decrease some episodes  
            excess = sum(lengths) - target_total
            for i in range(min(excess, n_episodes)):
                if lengths[i] > min_length:
                    lengths[i] -= 1
        
        # Check again
        actual_mean = sum(lengths) / n_episodes
        if target_mean_min <= actual_mean <= target_mean_max:
            return lengths

def assign_outcomes_per_episode(trials, min_rate=min_omission_rate, max_rate=max_omission_rate, target_overall=target_overall_omission_rate):
    
    outcomes = np.ones(len(trials))
    
    # Group trials by episode
    episodes = {}
    for i, trial in enumerate(trials):
        ep = trial['episode']
        if ep not in episodes:
            episodes[ep] = []
        episodes[ep].append(i)

    episode_rates = {}
    total_omissions_assigned = 0

    # Schritt 1: Für jede Episode exakte Anzahl basierend auf Episode-Rate bestimmen
    for episode_num, trial_indices in episodes.items():
        episode_length = len(trial_indices)
        
        # Zufällige Rate innerhalb der erlaubten Grenzen
        episode_rate = random.uniform(min_rate, max_rate)
        target_omissions = round(episode_length * episode_rate)
        
        # Strikt innerhalb min/max bounds halten
        min_allowed = max(1, round(episode_length * min_rate))
        max_allowed = round(episode_length * max_rate)
        target_omissions = max(min_allowed, min(max_allowed, target_omissions))

        # Valide Positionen bestimmen
        valid_indices = []
        for i in trial_indices:
            trial = trials[i]
            if trial['trial_in_episode'] <= 4:   # learning phase
                continue
            if trial['trial_in_episode'] == trial['episode_length']:  # last trial
                continue
            if i > 0 and trials[i]['cue_color'] != trials[i-1]['cue_color']:  # cue switch
                continue
            valid_indices.append(i)

        # Anzahl an verfügbare Positionen anpassen falls nötig
        if len(valid_indices) < target_omissions:
            print(f"[Warnung] Episode {episode_num}: nur {len(valid_indices)} gültige Positionen "
                  f"für {target_omissions} gewünschte Omissions")
            target_omissions = len(valid_indices)

        # Deterministische Auswahl ohne consecutive
        random.shuffle(valid_indices)
        selected = []
        for candidate in valid_indices:
            if all(abs(candidate - s) > 1 for s in selected):
                selected.append(candidate)
            if len(selected) >= target_omissions:
                break

        # Falls nicht genug non-consecutive Positionen verfügbar, fülle mit beliebigen auf
        if len(selected) < target_omissions:
            remaining_valid = [idx for idx in valid_indices if idx not in selected]
            needed = target_omissions - len(selected)
            random.shuffle(remaining_valid)
            selected.extend(remaining_valid[:needed])

        # Omissions setzen
        for idx in selected:
            outcomes[idx] = 0

        total_omissions_assigned += len(selected)
        actual_rate = len(selected) / episode_length if episode_length > 0 else 0
        episode_rates[episode_num] = actual_rate

        print(f"Episode {episode_num}: Ziel={target_omissions}, "
              f"gesetzt={len(selected)}, "
              f"Rate={actual_rate:.2%} (min={min_rate:.2%}, max={max_rate:.2%})")

    # Finale Statistiken
    overall_rate = total_omissions_assigned / len(trials)
    print(f"\n[Final] Gesamt: {total_omissions_assigned}/{len(trials)} "
          f"= {overall_rate:.2%}, Ziel={target_overall:.2%}")

    return outcomes, episode_rates, overall_rate

def assign_oddballs_per_episode(trials, outcomes, min_rate=min_oddball_rate, max_rate=max_oddball_rate, target_overall=oddball_rate):
    
    oddballs = np.zeros(len(trials))
    
    # Group trials by episode
    episodes = {}
    for i, trial in enumerate(trials):
        ep = trial['episode']
        if ep not in episodes:
            episodes[ep] = []
        episodes[ep].append(i)

    episode_targets = {}
    episode_assigned = {}
    episode_rates = {}
    episode_valid_indices = {}
    total_oddballs_assigned = 0

    # Schritt 1: pro Episode grobe Rate bestimmen
    for episode_num, trial_indices in episodes.items():
        episode_length = len(trial_indices)
        episode_rate = random.uniform(min_rate, max_rate)
        target_oddballs = round(episode_length * episode_rate)

        # min/max bounds
        min_possible = max(1, round(episode_length * min_rate))
        max_possible = round(episode_length * max_rate)
        target_oddballs = max(min_possible, min(max_possible, target_oddballs))

        episode_targets[episode_num] = target_oddballs

    # Schritt 2: oddballs tatsächlich zuweisen (ohne globales Balancing)
    for episode_num, trial_indices in episodes.items():
        episode_length = len(trial_indices)
        
        # Zufällige Rate innerhalb der erlaubten Grenzen
        episode_rate = random.uniform(min_rate, max_rate)
        target_oddballs = round(episode_length * episode_rate)
        
        # Strikt innerhalb min/max bounds halten
        min_allowed = max(1, round(episode_length * min_rate))
        max_allowed = round(episode_length * max_rate)
        target_oddballs = max(min_allowed, min(max_allowed, target_oddballs))

        # valide Positionen bestimmen (gleiche Restriktionen wie outcomes + keine outcome omissions + nicht vor outcome omissions)
        valid_indices = []
        for i in trial_indices:
            trial = trials[i]
            if trial['trial_in_episode'] <= 4:   # learning phase
                continue
            if trial['trial_in_episode'] == trial['episode_length']:  # letztes Trial
                continue
            if i > 0 and trials[i]['cue_color'] != trials[i-1]['cue_color']:  # cue switch
                continue
            if outcomes[i] == 0:  # bereits outcome omission
                continue
            if i+1 < len(outcomes) and outcomes[i+1] == 0:  # nächstes Trial ist outcome omission
                continue
            if i-1 >= 0 and outcomes[i-1] == 0:  # vorheriges Trial ist outcome omission
                continue
            valid_indices.append(i)

        if len(valid_indices) < target_oddballs:
            print(f"[Warnung] Episode {episode_num}: nur {len(valid_indices)} gültige Positionen "
                  f"für {target_oddballs} gewünschte Oddballs")
            target_oddballs = len(valid_indices)

        # deterministische Auswahl ohne consecutive
        random.shuffle(valid_indices)
        selected = []
        for candidate in valid_indices:
            if all(abs(candidate - s) > 1 for s in selected):
                selected.append(candidate)
            if len(selected) >= target_oddballs:
                break

        # Falls nicht genug non-consecutive Positionen verfügbar, versuche weniger strikt
        if len(selected) < target_oddballs:
            remaining_valid = [idx for idx in valid_indices if idx not in selected]
            needed = target_oddballs - len(selected)
            
            # Versuche erst noch non-consecutive zu finden
            for candidate in remaining_valid:
                if all(abs(candidate - s) > 1 for s in selected) and len(selected) < target_oddballs:
                    selected.append(candidate)
            
            # Falls immer noch nicht genug, reduziere das Ziel anstatt consecutive zu erlauben
            if len(selected) < target_oddballs:
                print(f"[Info] Episode {episode_num}: Reduziere Oddball-Ziel von {target_oddballs} auf {len(selected)} "
                      f"um consecutive Oddballs zu vermeiden")
                target_oddballs = len(selected)

        for idx in selected:
            oddballs[idx] = 1

        total_oddballs_assigned += len(selected)
        episode_assigned[episode_num] = len(selected)
        actual_rate = len(selected) / episode_length if episode_length > 0 else 0
        episode_rates[episode_num] = actual_rate

        print(f"Episode {episode_num}: Oddball Ziel={target_oddballs}, "
              f"gesetzt={len(selected)}, "
              f"Rate={actual_rate:.2%} (min={min_rate:.2%}, max={max_rate:.2%})")

    # Finale Statistiken ohne globales Balancing
    total_oddballs = int(np.sum(oddballs))
    overall_rate = total_oddballs / len(trials)

    print(f"\n[Final Oddball] Gesamt: {total_oddballs}/{len(trials)} "
          f"= {overall_rate:.2%}, Ziel={target_overall:.2%}")

    return oddballs, episode_rates, overall_rate

# Function to generate cue sequence for an episode
#===============================================================#

def generate_valid_cue_sequence(n_trials, required_start_color=None, required_end_color=None, episode_num=1, learning_phase_trials=0):
    
    for attempt in range(max_sequence_attempts):
        # Calculate number of trials per color (approximately half each -> 10 +/- 2 on average)
        n_color1 = random.randint(max(1, n_trials//2 - 2), min(n_trials-1, n_trials//2 + 2))
        n_color2 = n_trials - n_color1
        
        counts = {cue_colors[0]: 0, cue_colors[1]: 0}
        sequence = []
        
        # Handle learning phase trials at the start
        learning_trials_added = 0
        if learning_phase_trials > 0 and required_start_color:
            for i in range(min(learning_phase_trials, n_trials)):
                sequence.append(required_start_color)
                counts[required_start_color] += 1
                learning_trials_added += 1
        
        # Fill remaining positions
        remaining_positions = n_trials - learning_trials_added
        if required_end_color and remaining_positions > 0:
            remaining_positions -= 1  
        
        # Calculate remaining quota for each color
        remaining_color1 = n_color1 - counts[cue_colors[0]]
        remaining_color2 = n_color2 - counts[cue_colors[1]]
        
        # Adjust if end color requirement affects quota
        if required_end_color:
            if required_end_color == cue_colors[0]:
                remaining_color1 -= 1
            else:
                remaining_color2 -= 1
        
        # Generate middle section randomly while respecting quotas and streak limits
        temp_counts = {cue_colors[0]: remaining_color1, cue_colors[1]: remaining_color2}
        
        for pos in range(remaining_positions):
            available_colors = [c for c in cue_colors if temp_counts[c] > 0]
            
            # Enforce max streak constraint
            if len(sequence) >= max_same_color_streak:
                if all(color == sequence[-1] for color in sequence[-max_same_color_streak:]):
                    if sequence[-1] in available_colors:
                        available_colors.remove(sequence[-1])
            
            if not available_colors:
                break  # Failed this attempt, try again
            
            chosen_color = random.choice(available_colors)
            sequence.append(chosen_color)
            temp_counts[chosen_color] -= 1
        
        # Add required end color if specified
        if required_end_color and len(sequence) == n_trials - 1:
            sequence.append(required_end_color)
            counts[required_end_color] += 1
        
        # Verify the sequence meets all requirements
        if (len(sequence) == n_trials and 
            sequence.count(cue_colors[0]) == n_color1 and 
            sequence.count(cue_colors[1]) == n_color2 and
            (not required_start_color or sequence[0] == required_start_color) and
            (not required_end_color or sequence[-1] == required_end_color)):
            return sequence
    
    raise Exception(f"Could not generate valid sequence for episode {episode_num} after {max_sequence_attempts} attempts")
